articles.title: Fux suspende decisão de Dino e retoma determinação de Mendonça sobre posts de Nossa Senhora Aparecida | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro entendeu que os efeitos da decisão de Dino devem ficar suspensos até análise do caso pelo plenário do STF.
articles.summary: Ministro entendeu que os efeitos da decisão de Dino devem ficar suspensos até análise do caso pelo plenário do STF.
articles.body:
O ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) Luiz Fux suspendeu nesta segunda-feira (28) a decisão do ministro Flávio Dino que havia derrubado uma ordem do ministro André Mendonça, do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), para remover publicações que associavam o candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) à retirada de Nossa Senhora Aparecida do posto de padroeira do Brasil.

Com a decisão, Fux restabeleceu, até a análise pelo plenário do STF, as determinações de Mendonça para retirar do ar as postagens, que incluíam a uma publicação do humorista Antonio Tabet.

A decisão de Dino, tomada no domingo (27), havia permitido o restabelecimento do post de Tabet e de outras publicações removidas pelo mesmo fundamento . O ministro argumentou que a postagem não citava nominalmente Flávio Bolsonaro e que a medida era necessária para proteger a liberdade de expressão.

Segundo o ministro, o tema deve ser examinado pelo colegiado diante dos impactos sobre a Justiça Eleitoral e sobre a disputa presidencial em curso.

Na decisão, Fux afirmou ainda que não definiu quem tem razão sobre os limites da liberdade de expressão e lembrou, na decisão, do inquérito das fake news.

"Faz sentido que este Supremo Tribunal Federal determine a veiculação de notícia comprovadamente falsa? Não! Sob esse ângulo, medidas das mais autoritárias foram adotadas no âmbito dos inquéritos das fake news (Inq 4.781) e das 'milícias digitais' (Inq 4.874) sob o pretexto de coibir a desinformação, inclusive de coerção pessoal (prisão) e patrimonial", diz trecho da decisão.

Luiz Fux em sessão plenária do STF — Foto: Alejandro Zambrana/STF

O ministro também argumentou que a decisão de Dino suspendeu uma tutela concedida pela Justiça Eleitoral às vésperas do primeiro turno e permitiu a circulação de conteúdos que o TSE considerou baseados em uma informação sem respaldo nos fatos.

Fux determinou também que as plataformas digitais interrompam qualquer medida de execução da decisão de Dino e restabeleçam, em até 24 horas, a situação anterior, seguindo as ordens expedidas por Mendonça, no âmbito do TSE.

A controvérsia começou após a circulação, nas redes sociais, de publicações que associavam Flávio Bolsonaro e setores da direita a uma suposta iniciativa para retirar de Nossa Senhora Aparecida o título de padroeira do Brasil. O candidato negou a existência de qualquer proposta nesse sentido.

Na sexta-feira (25), Mendonça determinou a remoção de publicações relacionadas ao tema, entendendo que a narrativa não encontrava suporte na realidade e já havia sido corrigida publicamente. A decisão também autorizou que plataformas removessem réplicas do mesmo conteúdo considerado desinformativo.

No domingo (27), Dino derrubou essa ordem ao atender a um pedido apresentado por Tabet.

Nesta segunda (28), a defesa de Flávio Bolsonaro recorreu ao STF e pediu a suspensão da decisão.

Horas depois, Fux acolheu o pedido e restabeleceu os efeitos das determinações do TSE até que o plenário do Supremo analise o tema.

articles.title: O que pode e o que não pode levar para a urna no dia da eleição? | G1
articles.standfirst: É proibido entrar na cabine de votação com celular e portar armamentos a menos cem metros da seção eleitoral. Veja os outros critérios estabelecidos pela Justiça Eleitoral.
articles.summary: É proibido entrar na cabine de votação com celular e portar armamentos a menos cem metros da seção eleitoral. Veja os outros critérios estabelecidos pela Justiça Eleitoral.
articles.body:
Urna eletrônica. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Para conseguir registrar o seu voto é preciso seguir alguns critérios estabelecidos pela Justiça Eleitoral. Além de ser proibido entrar na cabine portando celular ou qualquer equipamento de que possa comprometer o sigilo do voto, os eleitores não podem se manifestar de maneira coletiva, bem como promover aglomerações usando vestuário padronizado .

A regra também vale para os mesários , que são impedidos de usar vestimentas ou objetos que caracterizem propaganda de partido político, federação, coligação ou candidatos. Distribuir camisetas, descartar panfletos em vias públicas e fazer boca de urna (toda e qualquer propaganda eleitoral) também são vetados no dia da eleição.

No entanto, o eleitor pode se manifestar de maneira individual e silenciosa , usando camisetas, bandeiras, broches, emblemas e adesivos. A famosa "cola" também é permitida e o eleitor pode entrar na cabine levando consigo um papel com anotações ou o "santinho político".

Posso votar de bermuda e chinelo? A resposta é simples: sim . As regras determinadas pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) não proíbem a utilização de nenhum dos dois itens.

No entanto, convém ficar atento: é proibido entrar nas zonas eleitorais sem camisa ou trajando roupas de banho, como biquíni, maiô ou sunga .

Também é permitido pedir ajuda aos mesários, mas somente a respeito da ordem de votação, nunca sobre o voto. Caso seja necessário, o eleitor com deficiência ou mobilidade reduzida pode ser auxiliado por pessoa de sua escolha, sendo permitido inclusive que o ajudante digite os números na urna. O auxiliar deverá se identificar perante a mesa receptora de votos.

É proibido o porte de armamento a menos de 100 metros da seção eleitoral , mesmo que possua porte legal de armas ou licença estatal. Só será permitido aos integrantes das forças de segurança quando autorizados ou convocados pela autoridade eleitoral competente.

Em 2026, continua valendo a unificação do horário de votação em todo o país. Segundo o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), todas as seções eleitorais funcionarão das 8h às 17h, no fuso horário de Brasília. Portanto, cidades em fusos diferentes devem se adequar ao horário da capital federal.

articles.title: Quaest, 2º turno: veja variação de Lula x Flávio Bolsonaro em setembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamentos ao longo do mês anterior à eleição mostram mudanças na distância entre os candidatos em alguns segmentos e recuperações, enquanto outros mantiveram cenários mais estáveis.
articles.summary: Levantamentos ao longo do mês anterior à eleição mostram mudanças na distância entre os candidatos em alguns segmentos e recuperações, enquanto outros mantiveram cenários mais estáveis.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta segunda-feira (28) mostra Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT) em empatados em eventual cenário de 2º turno. Os dois candidatos têm 42%, segundo o levantamento encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo.

Nos recortes por segmentos, houve variação ao longo do último mês antes do 1º turno. Entre as mulheres, por exemplo, a vantagem de Lula sobre Flávio caiu de 10 para 3 pontos e voltou a 9. No Sudeste, Flávio ampliou a vantagem de 8 para 16 pontos, mas terminou o mês 6 pontos à frente, em empate técnico.

Lula também ampliou a vantagem entre eleitores de menor renda e católicos. Entre os que ganham até dois salários mínimos, a diferença passou de 22 para 26 pontos, com 55% a 29%. Entre os católicos, o cenário de liderança se manteve, mas Lula foi de 46% para 50% ao longo do mês.

Veja as maiores variações nos grupos sociais ao longo de setembro:

Mulheres: Lula viu vantagem sobre Flávio ir de 10 pontos para 3 no meio do mês, quando voltou a recuperar a liderança no segmento e terminou o mês com 46% a 37%;

Sudeste: Flávio tinha 8 pontos a mais do que Lula, ampliou para 16 no meio do mês, mas viu o petista diminuir para 6 no levantamento mais recente, o que faz com que os dois estejam em empate técnico no limite da margem de erro, que é de 3 pontos;

Idade: Flávio liderava entre os mais jovens (16 a 34 anos) com 13 pontos a mais, já Lula tinha 17 a mais entre os mais velhos (60 anos ou mais) no início do mês. Agora, eles empatam em todas as faixas etárias -- entre os de 35 a 59 anos, Lula segue numericamente à frente por 2 pontos;

Ensino Fundamental: Lula subiu de 14 pontos para 23 pontos a mais do que Flávio: 54% a 31%;

Ensino Superior: empate técnico (44% Flávio, 40% Lula) virou vantagem para o senador, que está 15 pontos à frente do petista: 49% a 34%.

Até 2 salários mínimos: mais pobres ampliaram as intenções de voto em Lula, com diferença passando de 22 pontos (51% a 29%) para 26 (55% a 29%);

Brancos: Flávio estava 14 pontos distante de Lula e viu o presidente diminuir para 8 pontos;

Pardos: vantagem de Lula para Flávio, que era de 11 pontos, abaixou para 6 e entrou no empate técnico no limite da margem de erro.

❗ O empate técnico acontece quando a diferença entre os candidatos está dentro do intervalo da margem de erro. Nos casos abaixo, essa margem varia conforme o tamanho do segmento, sempre para mais e para menos. Clique aqui para saber mais sobre margem de erro .

Ao longo do mês, Lula dividiu a agenda entre atos oficiais e de campanha, com maior presença no Sudeste na reta final. O presidente anunciou um reajuste do Bolsa Família, assinou uma medida provisória que proibiu as bets e os jogos de cassino online, como o “Tigrinho”, e discursou na Assembleia da ONU, onde defendeu a soberania nacional ao afirmar que “o Brasil não cabe no quintal de ninguém”.

Flávio Bolsonaro, por sua vez, cumpriu agendas no Nordeste e anunciou a entrada do Brasil no Escudo das Américas, grupo criado pelo presidente americano Donald Trump para combater o crime organizado na América Latina. O candidato do PL também enfrentou uma polêmica envolvendo Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

O Caso Master passou a ser explorado pelos dois candidatos com mais ênfase: Lula buscando associar Flávio a Daniel Vorcaro, enquanto o candidato do PL destaca as relações do banqueiro com políticos e ministros do STF e tenta vincular o presidente a Alexandre Moraes, que teria trocado mensagens com o banqueiro.

A Quaest ouviu 2.004 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 24 e 27 de setembro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa é BR-06520/2026.

Presidente Lula e o senador Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert/Presidência da República; Vittor Sales

No Sudeste, Flávio tinha vantagem de 8 pontos no início do mês, alcançou 16 no meio do mês e viu Lula empatar tecnicamente no levantamento desta semana: 43% a 37%. Veja abaixo:

Quaest: intenções de voto no 2º turno entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) - Região — Foto: Arte/g1

Lula perdeu vantagem para Flávio entre as mulheres no meio do mês, quando houve empate técnico entre os dois, e se recuperou na pesquisa mais recentes. O presidente manteve vantagem sobre o senador: 9 pontos. Veja abaixo:

Quaest: intenções de voto no 2º turno entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) - Gênero — Foto: Arte/g1

Lula e Flávio estão tecnicamente empatados em todos os segmentos. Antes, Flávio liderava entre os mais jovens (16 a 34 anos), enquanto Lula, entre os mais velhos (60 anos ou mais). Veja abaixo:

Entre os eleitores com ensino fundamental, a vantagem de Lula sobre Flávio passou de 14 para 23 pontos, de 49% a 35% para 54% a 31%. Entre os mais escolarizados, o empate técnico no começo do mês (44% para Flávio, 40% a Lula) virou vantagem de 15 pontos para Flávio (49% a 34%). Já entre aqueles que tem ensino médio completo, a vantagem de Flávio subiu de 10 pontos (36% a 46%) para 15 (49% a 34%). Veja abaixo:

Os mais pobres (até 2 SM) aumentaram as intenções de voto em Lula: a vantagem do presidente sobre Flávio passou de 22 pontos (51% a 29%) para 26 (55% a 29%). Entre os mais ricos (mais de 5 SM), mantiveram mais apoiadores de Flávio, com vantagem de 15 (50% a 35%) para 18 pontos (52% a 34%) entre o começo e o fim de setembro. Vantagem de Flávio sobre Lula entre eleitores brancos foi de 14 pontos (48% a 34%), em 2 de setembro, para 8 (45% a 37%) nesta semana. Já Lula viu os 18 pontos (49% a 31%) à frente do adversário entre pretos irem a 13 (47% a 34%). articles.title: e-Título: veja como usar o aplicativo para votar nas Eleições 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: O e-título é um aplicativo da Justiça Eleitoral que permite obter a via digital do título de eleitor. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: O e-título é um aplicativo da Justiça Eleitoral que permite obter a via digital do título de eleitor. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.body:
Para votar no 1º turno das Eleições 2026, o eleitor pode usar o e-Título, aplicativo oficial da Justiça Eleitoral que funciona como a versão digital do título de eleitor.

O aplicativo também pode ser usado como documento de identificação com foto para votar, desde que o eleitor tenha feito o cadastramento biométrico e sua fotografia apareça no perfil do app.

Se você não tiver foto no e-Título, ainda poderá votar apresentando RG, identidade social, CNH (Carteira Nacional de Habilitação), passaporte, certificado de reservista ou carteira de trabalho ou de categoria profissional reconhecida por lei.

O aplicativo e-Título poderá ser baixado inclusive no dia da votação nas eleições de 2026, tanto no 1º quanto no 2º turno, em 4 e 25 de outubro. O anúncio foi feito na quinta-feira (24) pelo presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), o ministro Kassio Nunes Marques.

O e-Título está disponível gratuitamente e pode ser baixado em celulares ou tablets Android ( neste link ) e iOs ( neste link ).

No primeiro acesso, é necessário informar os dados pessoais e responder a perguntas para confirmem a identidade do eleitor para habilitar o e-Título.

Ao confirmar os dados solicitados, o aplicativo deverá solicitar a sua senha. Caso esta senha já tenha sido cadastrada nos anos anteriores, basta digitá-la e clicar em "Confirmar".

Se a senha estiver desatualizada ou não tiver sido criada anteriormente, o e-Título deverá pedir para que uma nova senha seja cadastrada.

O eleitor deve ficar atento ao prazo para baixar o e-título digital. A primeira via do aplicativo não pode ser emitida no dia da votação. Ou seja, o download só é permitido até 03 de outubro de 2026, um dia antes do primeiro turno das eleições.

articles.title: ‘UP is my karmabhoomi’: Former IAS officer Divya Mittal announces independent political entry
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Former IAS officer Divya Mittal on Tuesday announced that she would enter politics independently, saying Uttar Pradesh was her “karmabhoomi” and
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Former IAS officer Divya Mittal on Tuesday announced that she would enter politics independently, saying Uttar Pradesh was her “karmabhoomi” and the state would be the starting point of her political journey.In a video statement, Mittal said her decision grew out of what she had seen during her administrative career. “I realised that many problems of the public do not get resolved even when approvals, funds and provisions are in place,” she said. “There are people whose voices do not reach the government, and even when they do, their problems remain unheard.”She cited the example of a remote village where residents had sought a school offering education beyond Class V. Mittal said she approved the proposal, but construction had not begun years later. “It was not a question of funds or rules. There was a lack of intent,” she said.She also referred to a landless beneficiary who had official documents for an allotted plot but, she said, had not received physical possession.“Inquiries found irregularities in the reports, and corrective action was taken. Yet the work did not move forward,” Mittal said, questioning what she described as “higher-level interference” in cases where people were legally entitled to relief.Mittal said she wanted to take up issues including poor rural infrastructure, unsafe roads, examination paper leaks and employment concerns in the age of artificial intelligence. These, she said, needed greater public debate and attention from policymakers.“I want politics of intent, justice, concern and long-term thinking,” she said. “My objective is not just to replace political leaders. It is to change the way politics functions," she added.Rejecting speculation that she might join an existing party, Mittal said she would work directly with citizens and build an independent platform. She alleged that false political rumours circulated after her resignation were intended to discourage newcomers from entering public life. “I will not be deterred from raising public issues,” she said.Mittal appealed to people from different walks of life, including teachers, farmers, students, doctors, labourers and lawyers, to join her effort. “Meaningful political change can come only through collective public participation,” she said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: The Memo: Slew of Trump controversies gives headache to Republicans in midterms
articles.summary: There are just five weeks left until Election Day, and President Trump’s propensity for generating controversy is undimmed — much to the chagrin of some in his own party. Poll after poll shows Trump’s approval ratings to be low, with voters voicing concern about the cost of living, the economy and the war on Iran.…
articles.body:
There are just five weeks left until Election Day, and President Trump’s propensity for generating controversy is undimmed — much to the chagrin of some in his own party.

Poll after poll shows Trump’s approval ratings to be low, with voters voicing concern about the cost of living, the economy and the war on Iran.

But the Trump furors that have dominated recent days are drawn from a whole different realm.

Over the weekend, Trump’s ambassador to China told “Fox News Sunday” that the president had asked Chinese President Xi Jinping during his recent visit if he would like to purchase some U.S. armaments. It was a startling claim, given Beijing’s status as America’s most dangerous rival.

Also over the weekend, it emerged that a Trump campaign ad from early 2024 was getting another turn on the nation’s airwaves but this time “paid for by the U.S. government.” It is at least the second Trump-centric ad to receive taxpayer funding, provoking uproar.

Meanwhile, the president’s row with the media rumbles on, despite a judge last week issuing a temporary restraining order halting Trump’s proposed ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.

Other recent spats include turmoil at Washington’s Kennedy Center and the president’s suggestion that the large arch he wishes to erect near the National Mall should also “have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”

Monday was, as of 6 p.m. EDT, a relatively quiet day on the Trump-furor front, though he did find time to call Canada “one of the worst countries in the entire world” — seemingly a reference to trade policy with the U.S. — as he spoke with reporters in the Oval Office.

Virtually nobody in politics is surprised that Trump continues to spark controversy, often on a whim. But plenty of Republicans are irked by the president’s apparent inability to curb those instincts even at a critical juncture for the party.

“Those self-created outrages du jour distract the media’s attention and ultimately don’t help any Republican who is on the ballot,” said Doug Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee.

Referencing Republican Senate candidates in competitive races in Iowa and North Carolina, Heye added: “If you are Ashley Hinson or Michael Whatley, you want to be talking all day, every day, about what matters to your campaign. This makes it harder to do that.”

Hinson was in the Oval Office with Trump on Monday as he announced a company’s plans to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa.

Meanwhile, other GOP officeholders are making their feelings known about the latest controversies. On Sunday, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) was asked about one of the pro-Trump ads paid for by the government.

“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump … should spend public money on private ads for themselves. Now, the White House sees it differently,” Kennedy told CBS’s “Face the Nation” anchor Margaret Brennan.

The White House does indeed see it differently, including on its official website .

It brands attacks on the ads “highly dishonest,” insists the commercials are not campaign ads since Trump is not on the ballot — though he has told supporters to vote as if he is — and classifies them as “public service announcements.”

Separately, the row sparked by U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue reverberates. On Sunday, Perdue said, regarding American armaments, that Trump “actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

Asked about that alleged comment in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump denied making such a remark , saying, “I never heard of that one.” But he added : “They’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than them. So maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss it.”

Whatever the truth of the matter, Democrats feel that such episodes have the capacity to irk a large number of Americans, regardless of ideology.

“Who in this country doesn’t believe that China is our No. 1 foreign adversary — and we are going to sell them, to make a quick buck, the means to destroy us?” said Dick Harpootlian, a former chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party.

Harpootlian argued that Democrats’ most effective approach was not to promise impeachment or other punitive action toward Trump if they win back control of Congress in November but instead to offer themselves as a remedy for the chaos he often incites.

“When Democrats win, their first priority ought not to be creating a sideshow of impeachments or corruption investigations,” he said. “We need to get this country back on an even keel — financially, economically and morally.”

It is, of course, plausible that many of these controversies will pass quickly, as they tend to do in the Trump era.

There was already one such instance on Saturday, when White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino posted a short AI-generated video of himself, Eric Trump and their spouses jubilantly partying and being met with open arms by the president. The clip drew criticism online for being tone-deaf, but the storm soon passed.

Even with the bigger furors around Trump himself, some GOP strategists remain skeptical that they will play a major role in voters’ decisions.

“With most of these things, if it happened under any other administration, it would be the story of the month. But with Trump, most of these things are micro-controversies,” Republican strategist Dan Judy said. “They are baked into most voters’ calculations.”

But Judy acknowledged that the president’s penchant for turmoil has the capacity to drag GOP candidates off the territory they would prefer to fight on.

“Every candidate gets asked about these things over and over,” he said. “No candidate wants to be out there talking about these issues when they want to be talking about the cost of living. So from that perspective, it is a distraction.”

articles.title: GOP senators push back on Trump’s taxpayer-funded ad
articles.summary: President Trump’s new government-funded ads pledging to “cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists” are getting strong pushback from Senate Republicans...
articles.body:
President Trump's new government-funded ads pledging to "cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists" are getting strong pushback from Senate Republicans who are warning the president not to use taxpayer money to promote himself in such a brazenly political way.

While Republicans generally approve of Trump's political message, they say using taxpayer dollars to fund a series of ads that closely resemble Trump's past campaign advertising right before the midterm elections is inappropriate.

"It's a great message, I like the message, but it shouldn't be paid for by taxpayer dollars," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday.

The White House, however, argues the ads — which ran over the weekend during "Fox News Sunday" and several college and NFL football games — are "very clearly not campaign ads" and instead "a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it's worth defending."

Republican senators are not buying that argument, and warn that it creates an improper appearance to be using taxpayer money to pay for television ads that could easily be confused with regular campaign ads, even though Trump himself is not on the ballot.

"It would not have been something that I would have done," said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.). "I know that the White House is not covered by the same guidance that we are, but it's not something I would have done."

"I just don't think it's right to be using taxpayer money in that way, particularly if it's tied to political campaigns," he added. "I think they need to rethink that strategy."

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said using taxpayer money to fund a television ad that's nearly identical to the ad that Trump posted to social media during his presidential campaign and echoes the rhetoric he has used at election-year rallies crosses a red line.

"We all know you're not supposed to use taxpayer money for that purpose," the Republican senator noted.

Cornyn said he doesn't know exactly where the money to produce and air the ads is coming from but added "if it comes from taxpayers, it shouldn't."

The latest advertisement, which ran on television over the weekend, is part of a series of ads that come with the disclaimer: "Paid by the U.S. Government."

It is nearly identical to an online ad that Trump posted to his Truth Social account in January 2024, when he was preparing to launch his presidential campaign. In that online ad, he urged supporters to text "TRUMP to 88022" to support his campaign.

The ad features Trump walking down hallway while an audio clip plays of a speech he delivered at an unidentified event pledging: "This is the final battle. With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state, we will expel the warmongers from our government. We will drive out the globalists, we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists."

"We will liberate America from these villains once and for all," Trump is heard declaring as an unseen audience cheers in the background.

The latest iteration of the ad, however, ends with a disclaimer informing viewers that it was "paid for by the U.S. government."

The White House aired its first ad of the new series last week — a 30-second television spot that featured a montage of pictures of the president, interspersed with Trump's declaration that "together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America" and that "America will never be a communist country."

The ad was paired with the song "Love Me" by JMSN and ended with a voiceover of UFC President Dana White extolling Trump as the "toughest, most resilient person I have ever met."

The White House responded to criticisms in a statement.

"The attacks on President Donald J. Trump's public service announcements are highly dishonest. The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action," the White House argued.

The White House noted that the George W. Bush administration ran a national television campaign explaining the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act to seniors — one of former President Bush's signature legislative accomplishments — in March 2004, when Bush was up for reelection later that year.

The White House also pointed out that the Obama administration used national advertising to promote subsidies under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) in 2015 and the start of open enrollment under the ACA in 2016.

Republican Sen. John Curtis (Utah) said constituents "are worried about affordability and they don't want to be worried about how their taxpayer dollars are being spent."

"If it were me as a senator, it would be a problem," he said of using taxpayer money to fund ads that appear to be political in nature.

"I don't know their rules as well as I know mine, but I know mine would prohibit that," he added.

A Senate GOP aide who requested anonymity to discuss the matter said the new Trump promotional ads paid for by the federal government appear "very similar" in nature to the promotional ads that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem ran last year to tout her leadership of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Trump fired Noem after she was grilled about the expenditure of public funds for the promotional ad blitz, which was estimated to cost more than $220 million.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy (La.), a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who challenged Noem over DHS's advertising campaign in March, said he disagreed with the Trump administration's use of public funds for the new series of ads.

"I don't think any public official, including President Trump … should spend public money on private ads for themselves," Kennedy said Sunday on CBS News's "Face the Nation."

"The White House sees it differently," he added.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called on the Justice Department to investigate whether the use of taxpayer money to pay for ads promoting rhetoric similar to what Trump has used at political events violates the law.

"There should be a full investigation because on its face it appears to be a violation of federal law," she said.

"The Department of Justice, the folks that enforce federal law, should be the ones" to lead the investigation, she said.

"This is the problem when the attorney general says his duty of loyalty is not to the people of the United States but instead is to Donald Trump personally," she added, referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Richard Painter, a White House ethics lawyer who served under Bush, wrote on social platform X that the use of taxpayer money to promote the president's political message shortly before the midterm election "could be an impeachable offense."

"@POTUS has no right to use taxpayer money for campaign ads. Congress has expressly prohibited government sponsored political propaganda, which is dangerous for democracy," he warned.

articles.summary: President Trump hopes the third time will be the charm as his latest round of tariffs heads to court this week. articles.body:
President Trump hopes the third time will be the charm as his latest round of tariffs heads to court this week.

The Supreme Court already ruled Trump can’t invoke an emergency statute to impose his global trade war. Now, the president is pointing to a different law, and this time, everyone agrees it allows the president to impose at least some tariffs.

But some of the very same small businesses are suing the administration again, advancing similar legal arguments.

It’s all set to come to a head Wednesday morning in New York City, when the U.S. Court of International Trade will take the bench.

“Rinse and repeat, baby!” said Rick Woldenberg, who leads the family-run educational toy company Learning Resources and is behind one of the leading lawsuits.

Trump has shifted gears after the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in February the president couldn’t impose his “Liberation Day” tariffs by invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

Now, the president points to the Trade Act of 1974. After invoking one of the law’s temporary authorities , those have expired, and the president has moved on to permanent tariffs under a provision known as Section 301.

The challengers say the judges shouldn’t fall for it.

“If it looks like an IEEPA tariff and it smells like an IEEPA tariff, it maybe is an IEEPA tariff,” said Sara Albrecht, CEO of the Liberty Justice Center. The libertarian public-interest firm was behind Trump’s Supreme Court defeat and is involved once again.

The Trump administration rejects the notion that it’s some dubious repackaging of the earlier, invalidated levies.

“The relative proximity of the imposition of Section 301 tariffs with the expiration of Section 122 tariffs shows, at most, that the Trump Administration continues to maintain that tariffs are beneficial to the American economy,” the Justice Department wrote in court filings.

“It is entirely permissible that the timing of an agency’s policymaking actions may be informed by Administration priorities,” it continued.

Section 301 authorizes the president to impose tariffs in response to unfair trade practices that are found to restrict the nation’s commerce. Trump has invoked it to add a surcharge between 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 economies, which account for the vast majority of imports.

The lawsuits filed by Albrecht’s firm and Woldenberg’s company say it’s a country-specific measure that must be more tailored than Trump’s sweeping announcement.

That argument got the backing of Alan Wm. Wolff, who served as the Treasury Department’s lead international trade lawyer in the Nixon administration and created the proposal that became Section 301. In an interview, he said Trump can’t bundle together the dozens of countries.

“Our problems were bilateral, and no one in the whole drafting of the Trade Act of 1974 ever mentioned — I was in all of the meetings — and no one ever mentioned it being a broad tariff authority. … It was how do you get the Japanese to open their market? How do you get the Europeans to allow in some of our agricultural products?” Wolff said.

The Trump administration points to the U.S. trade representative’s (USTR) investigations into forced labor overseas and says Section 301 provides Jamieson Greer and his office wide discretion to respond.

“But these are discretionary calls for USTR—not plaintiffs, and not this Court—to make. USTR’s determinations on that score were reasonable and reasonably explained,” the Justice Department wrote.

The small businesses will be joined by Democratic-controlled states Wednesday. But like the previous rounds of litigation, large corporations have declined to lead the lawsuits.

“Corporate America, where are you?” said Albrecht, the Liberty Justice Center’s CEO. “I always ask corporate America for help, support, amicus, anything — and not one larger company has stepped forward.” But for Woldenberg, an ex-lawyer, he said it was important to get his small business involved and declined to speculate on why big businesses were sitting out. He expressed concern that the public may not be keeping as close tabs.

“Now that it’s the third time around, this seems to be garnering less attention,” Woldenberg said. “And the only reason that that concerns me is the issues are no less important.”

articles.title: Socialist jeweler who called US a 's---hole' teams up with top Dem Senate hopefuls
articles.summary: Alexis Bittar, who called America a "s---hole" and the American flag a symbol of aggression, hosts a fundraiser in NYC supporting Democratic Party candidates for U.S. Senate.
articles.body: Democratic Senate candidates Sherrod Brown and James Talarico reportedly headlined a star-studded New York City fundraiser hosted by celebrity jewelry designer Alexis Bittar, whose recent public comments describe the United States as a "s---hole" and characterized the American flag as "a symbol of aggression." The fundraiser, held Monday evening in Manhattan, featured contribution levels ranging from $500 to $27,000 and also listed actor Robert De Niro among the high-powered hosts, according to an invitation cited by the Washington Free Beacon. Bittar's recent record includes a July interview during which he discussed his concerns about the country's future, while promoting a documentary centered on "reclaim[ing]" the American flag. During the interview, Bittar questioned what Americans were doing to create "the country we want to live in" before adding: "I have three kids, and they're little, and they're growing up in this s---hole. So if we don't do something now, we're f---ed." FIRST ON FOX: JAMES TALARICO SLAMMED FOR CALLING AMERICAN FLAG ‘COMPLICATED SYMBOL’ AHEAD OF INDEPENDENCE DAY The Free Beacon highlighted separate remarks Bittar made about the American flag while discussing the documentary, saying in an interview with Forbes in July 2025 that the American flag had become "a symbol of aggression" during President Donald Trump's political rise. "Thinking about the new administration and what actions I can take to combat their policies. It seemed folks were in shock and experiencing malaise. But I homed in how the flag was co-opted by the right and how did the left let that happen?" he said in the interview. "It’s become such a symbol of aggression, the American flag, like ‘we're coming for you’ during Trump’s era." Bittar has been active in progressive Democratic politics. Gothamist previously reported that he was among the donors who gave the maximum amount to support New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's transition and served on the mayor's Arts & Culture transition committee. He has also been unafraid of the "socialist" label, the Free Beacon reported. "Hey people … it’s voting time!!! Bringing in all the Democrat Socialists!! Let’s change America…!" he said while urging people to go out and vote for various candidates in New York several weeks ago on Instagram. Bittar also recently hosted a fundraiser for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, while in an August Instagram video with the U.S. Senate candidate from Michigan. Bittar declared that "the traditional Democrats have one foot in the grave" and that "the revolution has begun." TIM SCOTT GOES SCORCHED EARTH ON EL-SAYED: 'HE'S FOR HAMAS, BUT HE'S AGAINST AMERICA' Bittar's jewelry has been worn by celebrities including Michelle Obama, Beyoncé, Lady Gaga and Rihanna, and he has built a high-profile fashion brand while also becoming increasingly active in progressive Democratic politics. One of Bittar's past marketing campaigns featured a fictional female serial killer. While speaking with V Magazine about the campaign in December 2025, Bittar said he had "always [been] intrigued by people who kill" and said the project was intended to "raise the bar" for marketing. "I am always intrigued by people who kill, and I love to trace their own personal history and the trajectories that led them to become killers," Bittar said. "Meet Amanda Gates ... she is the most unlikely new fashion icon." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A spokesperson for Talarico's campaign declined to comment about the fundraiser, while neither Brown nor Bittar returned Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

articles.title: Trump to host summit with top AI leaders in Washington
articles.summary: The president has been skeptical of guardrails on artificial intelligence, wanting to stay ahead of China. He’ll also launch an AI-powered website, America.gov, on Tuesday.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — As he brushes aside artificial intelligence doomsday warnings as a “hoax,” President Donald Trump on Tuesday will host nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch to discuss the rapidly advancing technology. The group includes a who’s who of the tech world, including CEO of SpaceX and Tesla Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, according to a White House official. Trump is hosting the lunch with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also will be on hand. Earlier Tuesday, Trump unveiled America.gov, a website that features an AI-powered tool meant to serve as a “one-stop shop” for Americans navigating government services. In recent weeks, tech executives on the AI frontier, including Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, have sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI, calling for greater government oversight and global cooperation in regulating the technology. Trump has dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race. Trump isn’t expected to deviate from that AI messaging, even as the dire warnings about humans’ potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent. “Whoever wins AI ... whoever wins “SI,” whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins, and we’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump said in his address last week to the United Nations General Assembly. “I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution — many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet itself — and we will be very careful,” he said. Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic. Coxon warned that the people building those systems believe they could “kill us all by the end of the decade.” Johnson has made it clear he doesn’t believe Washington should take a heavy-handed approach to regulating AI, arguing that existing laws and regulations can be applied to AI companies and suggesting that they should be held legally liable if their products caused harm. In an appearance Monday on Fox Business, Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room. “They have a corporate responsibility, as every corporation does, to create safe products, right? And there’s product liabilities laws that apply and a labyrinth of federal regulations on all this stuff already. We do not need a moratorium,” he said. While lawmakers have introduced dozens of AI-related bills in recent years, the GOP-controlled Congress is showing no urgency to act on the issue. House members aren’t expected back in Washington until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and senators could leave town as soon as this week. “We do not need to jump in and hyperregulate this, because we’ll lose the race to China,” Johnson said on Fox Business. “The innovation is important to continue, but we have to strike the right balance.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he won’t attend the AI lunch, but he privately met with Amodei in the Capitol on Monday evening. “I hope it’s productive,” Thune said of Tuesday’s summit. Before the White House lunch, Trump gathered with Vance, Cabinet members and a handful of tech leaders a few blocks away at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium to unveil America.gov, an AI-powered web portal and chatbot designed to improve Americans’ experiences accessing federal resources. A White House official called the tool “a new front door for the federal government that will provide a one-stop shop for Americans looking for information and resources from the federal government that are currently spread over a maze of various agency websites.” The National Design Studio, the year-old agency launched by Trump and led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, helped create the project. Trump was introduced by self-help author and motivational speaker Tony Robbins. “We’re launching today something that is really — it’s not just simply a website; it’s a restoration of America’s founding promise, and it’s a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond,” Trump said. “Instead of forcing citizens to search through the endless maze of tens of thousands of terrible government websites and rules ... you’ll now have one front door for every single question,” Trump said. “Everything will be answered easily and quickly, a digital home built around your time and your life.” Trump likened the site to chatbots like Grok, Gemini and ChatGPT and a White House official told NBC News that America.gov is using Gemini and Grok. Trump also suggested he would “end” America.gov if it was ever hacked. It “cannot, in theory, be hacked into. And when they figure a way to do that, we’ll end it, okay?” Trump said. “Because they always figure a way, right?” In addition to Trump and Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz were on hand. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp were also expected to attend, according to the White House.

articles.title: Iran tells the US public that Trump's war has failed, and other Mideast developments
articles.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard urged Americans in a message ahead of U.S. midterm elections to take to the streets and rally against Donald Trump, claiming the U...
articles.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard urged Americans in a message ahead of U.S. midterm elections to take to the streets and rally against Donald Trump, claiming the U.S. president's war in the Middle East has failed.

Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank , settlers rioted, throwing rocks, blocking roads and setting Palestinian property on fire to prevent a Palestinian man escorted by the Israeli military from returning to his home in the village of Jalud.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Full coverage is available here .

An Iranian spokesman advises Americans to reconsider their leaders

Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for the Revolutionary Guard, held a news conference in Tehran, Iran's capital, on Tuesday and read from what he said was a "letter to the American people."

Reading from the prepared text, he said that the only way for the war to end is for Washington to admit defeat and leave. The message was apparently meant for the U.S. public just weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections for the U.S. Senate and Congress — a vote in which Trump's Republican Party faces fierce headwinds as it looks to maintain control of Congress.

Later, in remarks to The Associated Press, Mohebbi urged Americans to take to the streets and protest Trump's policies to denounce what he called the U.S. government's war-mongering policies.

Mohebbi also said Americans should "revise their decision" about their leaders.

He accused the United States of using Iran's nuclear program as a ruse to "plunder Iran's wealth" and to turn the country "back into a colony." The U.S. military action and economic sanctions would not get Tehran to submit.

Meanwhile, Iran's currency fell to a new record low Tuesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging more than 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar, a sign of how the conflict has further eroded Iran's economy.

The decline came after the rial hit its previous record low of 2.2 million to the dollar on Sept. 2. The currency has repeatedly reached new lows since the war began in February.

Settlers block a Palestinian man from returning to his West Bank home

Over a hundred Israeli settlers scuffled with Israeli soldiers who were trying to escort a Palestinian man to his home in the West Bank village of Jalud.

The homeowner, Mahmoud Tubasi, told the AP that the soldiers initially brought him to his home but that rioting settlers forced him to leave with his family in a military vehicle. He said he still can't access the house, which settlers have besieged for two months.

Israel's military acknowledged that the overnight mission to return the family "was not completed" and that three officers were injured by settlers who threw rocks, blocked roads and set Palestinian property on fire.

Israeli police said they arrested three settlers suspected of participating in the riot, which was condemned by Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Foreign Minister Gidon Saar and President Isaac Herzog.

The Israeli military has struggled to quell the latest wave of settler violence. Rights groups have accused the military of colluding with the settlers.

Israel says strike kills Hamas commander

An Israeli strike on an apartment west of Gaza City killed two people, including a Hamas commander who the Israeli military said was involved in plotting attacks and recruiting new members for the militant group.

Al-Shifa Hospital officials said Tuesday the strike also wounded five others.

Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz said the overnight strike targeted Izz al-Din Bik, a commander in the Hamas militant group's northern Gaza brigade.

Hamas confirmed the death of al-Bik, claiming in a statement he was one of the main overseers of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks on southern Israel, which killed over 1,200 and prompted the war in Gaza.

More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since a ceasefire took effect nearly a year ago, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, while over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began. The ministry maintains detailed records that are generally seen as reliable. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants, but says women and children make up around half of the fatalities.

Gaza refugee camp mourners hold mass funeral for dozens killed in war

A mass funeral was held Tuesday in Gaza's Nuseirat refugee camp for nearly 50 people killed during the war.

The remains, wrapped in white bags and draped with Palestinian flags, were recovered last week from the rubble of buildings destroyed almost three years ago.

Mass funerals have become more common in Gaza, where Israel has not allowed the heavy machinery needed to clear the rubble of destroyed buildings and recover the dead.

Earlier this month, the United Nations estimated that more than 8,000 bodies remain buried under the debris.

For some, partial remains were all they had to bury.

Areej Farajallah said two of her husband's bones were found last week. She is also mourning her child, who was among those buried Tuesday.

Abdel-Nasser al-Tawil said his home was hit Oct. 15, 2023, in the early days of the war. He said he recovered 13 bodies Tuesday with the help of the Red Cross and Palestinian Civil Defense workers ahead of the funeral.

articles.title: Trump kicks off week with economic ‘win’ for Iowa
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Trump touts Iowa steel mill ▪ Education Department strikes LGBTQ protections ▪ Backlash to government-funded ads ▪ Iran denies involvement in U.K. incident President Trump unveiled plans for a Minnesota company to build a new $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, kicking off the week with a dose of positive economic news as…
articles.body:
▪ Education Department strikes LGBTQ protections

▪ Iran denies involvement in U.K. incident

President Trump unveiled plans for a Minnesota company to build a new $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, kicking off the week with a dose of positive economic news as the GOP contends with weakening polls just five weeks out from the midterms.

Trump made the announcement alongside executives from Mesabi Metallics, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Republican Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Ashley Hinson , who are facing competitive races for House reelection and for Senate, respectively.

“There’s a company known as Mesabi,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “And they’re going to make a big investment in a place called Iowa. I love Iowa. I won Iowa every time. Today, we’re thrilled to announce that Mesabi Metallics will be building the largest steel plant in American history in the great state of Iowa.”

The White House said the mill would be the first mega-steel plant to be built in the U.S. since the 1960s. It is expected to begin operating in 2030 and eventually create 1,750 jobs in Iowa.

Iowa is among the handful of historically red states that have become competitive in 2026, as Democrats increasingly see control of the Senate as within reach.

The Hill’s Mallory Wilson reports that because of the tight races, Republicans from the Hawkeye State have had to weigh just how much they want to tie themselves to the president and his administration.

Hinson skipped Vice President Vance’ s trip to Iowa earlier this month, though her campaign cited a scheduling conflict. She has been among the loudest voices calling for federal action to address rising diesel prices.

Miller-Meeks was among the seven Republicans, and two vulnerable Iowa House members, to vote this month to block Trump from continuing the Iran war without first seeking congressional approval.

Since January, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, GOP approval on Trump’s handling of the economy fell from 80 percent to 56 percent and fell from 70 percent to 44 percent on his handling of the cost of living.

“Right now, the races are — it’s more about — it’s, you know, it is affordability issues, it’s the price of diesel in places like Iowa and Kansas and Nebraska and the Midwest, Minnesota,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said yesterday on Fox News’s “America’s Newsroom.”

“I think that’s the issue,” he added. “ And what’s happening, Iran [has] sort of trumped everything else that’s going on.”

Trump is reportedly considering a pause or partial ban on exporting diesel fuel, though some key voices in the administration are opposed to it.

The Iowa plant marks Trump’s latest effort to revitalize domestic steel manufacturing after levying steel tariffs during his first term and increasing them to 50 percent last year.

Steel prices in America are some of the highest in the world, raising costs for businesses that rely on steel to produce goods. But steel-industry trade groups have pressed Trump not to weaken tariffs, The Wall Street Journal reported , crediting them with drawing more than $40 billion in investments and creating thousands of new jobs.

“President Trump is delivering on his promise to rebuild American industry, reshore manufacturing, and create new jobs. Today’s announcement underscores the President’s historic efforts to revitalize the U.S. steel industry,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement.

▪ The Hill : New polls have Democrats thinking big on Senate.

▪ The Hill : Trump approval slips to historic low in Wall Street Journal survey.

Trump denied discussing arms sales to China during his meeting last week with Chinese President Xi Jinping, breaking with U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue’s comments on Sunday. Trump said China would probably want to buy U.S. weapons and it may be a “good idea,” but it wasn’t discussed.

FBI Deputy Director Andrew Bailey said that he is leaving the bureau after about a year in the role , planning to return to his family in Missouri. Bailey first shared his title with Dan Bongino, who stepped down in January, and then Christopher Raia, who has served since then.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth instructed the Pentagon to deploy “advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities” to defend the upcoming midterms from foreign actors. He directed the head of U.S. Cyber Command to coordinate with the Department of Homeland Security to counter possible cyber threats.

FILE – The headquarters of the U.S. Department of Education, March 12, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein, File)

CARVED OUT : The Education Department formally rescinded a Biden-era Title IX interpretation Monday that provided sex-based discrimination protections to students based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The change will require schools to return to Title IX rules as they were interpreted under the first Trump administration in 2020. The president had vowed to end the protections while on the campaign trail in 2024.

When the Biden administration rolled out the protections in 2024, officials restored Obama-era interpretations that the definition of sex discrimination under Title IX applies to cover sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Trump administration overturned former President Obama ’s interpretation during his first term and has now done so again with former President Biden ’s interpretation during his second term.

The Education Department said the move will protect women’s sports.

“We will continue to relentlessly champion equal opportunity for all Americans and hold accountable any school or college that violates the rights, privacy, or athletic opportunities of our women and girls,” Education Secretary Linda McMahon said.

The Biden-era rule had already been struck down by a federal judge last fall following a lawsuit from a group of 15 Republican-led states.

The Title IX change wasn’t the only move on LGBTQ rights that the administration made Monday. It also asked the Supreme Court to lift a judge’s block on its policy restricting transgender inmates’ access to hormone treatments and gender-affirming surgeries.

Before the Supreme Court starts its new term next week, it will hear the Trump administration’s latest appeal on Wednesday defending the president’s authority to issue widespread tariffs.

The court already blocked his authority invoking one law, but now as The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld reports for Insider, the administration is attempting to get a green light under a separate statute. “Rinse and repeat, baby!” said one of the litigants. Sign up for Insider and click the link here to read his rundown.

▪ Washington Blade : U.N. human rights chief sounds alarm on ‘onslaught’ against LGBTQ rights.

ROLLING BACK : The administration also on Monday pulled back car efficiency standards requiring automakers to ensure their cars and lightweight trucks use less fuel.

Standards adopted during the Biden administration expected to have the country’s car fleet average 50.4 miles per gallon by 2031. The Trump administration lowered the number to 34.9 miles per gallon.

It argued that the move would make new cars $1,300 cheaper on average, though critics argue owners could pay more on gasoline as a result, in addition to worsening pollution and climate change.

Biden’s regulations were already undermined by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which lowered the penalty imposed on automakers that don’t comply to $0.

▪ The Hill : Samuel Alito recuses from major climate case.

▪ The Hill : House Republican says Americans feel ‘fatigue’ in rising diesel prices.

OVER THE FINISH LINE : The Senate approved a landmark college sports bill Monday night in a 77-22 vote, sending it to the House for consideration after tense negotiations.

The Protect College Sports Act would implement a wide range of rules as part of new federal oversight for the NCAA, including granting student athletes a new federal right to earn compensation for their name, image and likeness. It would cap agents’ fees at 5 percent, guarantee scholarships for 10 years after eligibility and allow athletes to transfer once without having to sit out for a year.

It would also protect the NCAA from antitrust lawsuits and prevent coaches from leaving midseason to coach or take over another program during the same season, among other measures. The legislation’s passage marks a rare bipartisan success as it received sweeping support across the aisle.

The final vote came after senators voted down a series of amendments, including provisions that would have limited increases in ticket prices that schools can charge for major sporting events and capped coaches’ salaries.

But the true hurdle for the bill may now come in the House, where it’s facing more opposition . Critics of the legislation have called it a gift to the NCAA and top conferences, allowing them to stifle the earning potential of the student athletes, especially minorities.

With the House out of session until after the midterms, the lower chamber isn’t expected to take up the bill until later this fall.

▪ Semafor : Ted Cruz wants Republicans to campaign on the bill.

▪ NPR : Athletes-turned-senators have a seat at the table.

ONWARD : Major television networks will continue to provide pool coverage of the president’s daily activities this week despite the White House’s efforts to block CNN from covering him.

Coverage resumed late last week after CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back onto the White House grounds following a federal judge’s ruling blocking Trump’s banning of the three outlets from the building. But tensions popped up again after CNN was blocked from covering Trump on Air Force One ahead of his trip to Tennessee for a college football game.

A person familiar with the discussions told The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo that the networks are assessing the TV pool situation on a day-by-day basis. The major networks, which includes NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News, banned together last week in response to the bans, pulling out of pool coverage.

A White House schedule for TV pool rotation announced Sunday listed CNN as the primary pooler for Thursday, when Trump is scheduled to visit Texas and Oklahoma for rallies.

▪ The New York Times : A 7-day standoff that said so much about Trump, the media.

The president will make an announcement about America.gov at 10 a.m. He will participate in a meeting and luncheon on artificial intelligence at 12:30 p.m. and sign executive orders at 5 p.m.

Donald Trump, then the GOP candidate for president, speaks at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio., Sept. 17, 2022. (AP Photo/Tom E. Puskar, File)

NOT OK : Republican senators are pushing back on the president’s new government-funded ads, warning that taxpayer funds shouldn’t be used for such brazen self-promotion.

The Trump administration has now released a few different ads made with government funding in which Trump is heard pledging to “cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists.” The White House has said the ads, which aired during “Fox News Sunday” and several college and professional football games, are “very clearly not campaign ads.”

It said the ads are just a “reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending.”

But The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports that GOP senators aren’t buying that argument, warning that the ads create an improper appearance using taxpayer dollars for promotions that could be easily confused with regular campaign ads.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) noted that the latest ad is nearly identical to one that Trump posted to social media during his reelection campaign, arguing it crosses a red line.

The White House noted that the George W. Bush administration ran a national TV campaign explaining one of his signature legislative accomplishments in March 2004 as he was running for reelection and the Obama administration used national advertising to promote subsidies under the Affordable Care Act.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said constituents are concerned about affordability and don’t “want to be worried about how their taxpayer dollars are being spent.”

“I don’t know their [the White House’s] rules as well as I know mine, but I know mine would prohibit that,” he said.

▪ CNN : Trump personally helped orchestrate the taxpayer-funded ads.

▪ The Hill : Former White House ethics lawyer says ads could be ‘impeachable offense.’

A B1 bomber is towed past another B1 aircraft at RAF Fairford, a US airforce base in Fairford, England, Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant)

NOT US : Iran strongly denied any involvement in what authorities say was a foiled terrorist attack attempt on a U.S.-operated air base in England.

The Iranian embassy in London said Monday in a post on the social platform X that it “categorically rejects” the “unfounded and malicious speculations” that link Tehran to the individuals detained near the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford air base the day before.

All five men, who are from London and range in age from 23 to 25 years old, were released on bail Monday but remain under investigation. They were initially arrested on explosives and terror charges after three vans considered suspicious were located outside the base.

Laurence Taylor , the head of Britain’s counterterrorism police, told reporters that the men’s release is subject to “stringent conditions” on their movement and contact with others. He did not say whether investigators had found explosives in any of the vans and didn’t take questions.

A robot used to dispose of explosives was used to inspect the vans, but it’s unclear if anything was found.

Taylor said detectives are investigating from “every possible angle,” including that this may have been perpetrated by proxies working on behalf of a “foreign state.”

Trump said he didn’t agree with the release of the suspects on bail.

Meanwhile, negotiations are ongoing as mediators work behind the scenes with Iran and the U.S. to reach a deal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump rejected Iran’s latest ceasefire proposal over the weekend.

▪ The Hill : Trump ‘surprised’ by release of the five men.

▪ The Hill Insider : Cuba tensions on the rise as Trump pushes for change.

Despite popular narratives, free speech is working in Macklemore’s favor , Steven Lubet writes in The Hill.

Democrats have already proven we can deliver on affordability , Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-Md.) writes in The Hill.

Actresses Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, from left, join Country Music singer Dolly Parton, right, in front of a mural advertising their motion picture “9 to 5” at the premiere night in Beverly Hills, Calif., on December 12, 1980. (AP Photo)

And finally … Weeks after Dolly Parton ’s death, her classic movie “9 to 5” will return to theaters next month for a one-week run.

NewsNation reported that a newly restored version of the film, which also stars Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin , will be shown in theaters nationwide from Oct. 9-15.

Disney will donate net proceeds from each U.S. ticket purchase to the Dollywood Foundation, the nonprofit that Parton created in the late 1980s to improve children’s education and literacy, Deadline reported . Proceeds will be used to support her Imagination Library, a program that gives free books to children across the country.

The country music star known as the “Queen of Country” died last month at the age of 80 after a battle with cancer.

articles.title: We need accountability for federal employee purges made on false pretenses
articles.summary: I was grilling chicken on a sweltering summer night in the Washington, D.C. suburbs, when I peeked at my phone and saw that a senior official in the administration had just accused me of lying to Congress. This was unpleasant but unsurprising. MAGA acolytes had spent years vilifying the work I did in government to…
articles.body:
I was grilling chicken on a sweltering summer night in the Washington, D.C. suburbs, when I peeked at my phone and saw that a senior official in the administration had just accused me of lying to Congress.

This was unpleasant but unsurprising. MAGA acolytes had spent years vilifying the work I did in government to fight foreign propaganda and disinformation. When they gained power, they shuttered my office and fired most of my colleagues. They finally pushed me out of the State Department a few weeks ago.

The campaign against us grew out of broader allegations about a so-called “censorship industrial complex” — a cabal of bureaucrats, progressive activists, and tech industry insiders who had supposedly conspired to censor conservatives online.

In April 2025, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio closed our office — known for most of its existence as the Global Engagement Center — he falsely alleged that it had been deeply involved in that supposed conspiracy. He claimed that we had “spent millions of dollars to actively silence and censor the voices of Americans they were supposed to be serving.”

To put it bluntly, no evidence at all supports that smear. More than 30 civil servants who had done nothing wrong lost their jobs. Offices with the same mission at the Department of Homeland Security, FBI and in the intelligence community met similar fates.

As a result, dozens of programs to fight Russian disinformation, Chinese propaganda, and Iranian cognitive warfare came to an end.

The effects have already made themselves felt. Global perceptions of the U.S. have nosedived, with more and more people in key regions viewing China favorably . Beijing is actively injecting its perspective using chatbots. Russia continues to wage hybrid war against the west. Iran is using AI-generated Lego videos to shape the global narrative.

The purge of civil servants is not the only reason for these shifts, but it has been an undeniable factor.

President Trump’s political fortunes are now on the wane, raising the prospect of investigations and hearings. We may soon have a chance to start repairing the damage that politically motivated purges inflicted on our national security, but a positive outcome will require scrupulous preparation and careful execution.

Scholars have defined a “purge” as an attempt to remove a perceived political threat from within government. Stalinist purges aimed to sow terror through the physical liquidation of individuals. Nothing so extreme has happened in America. But firings justified with murky rhetoric about “deep state” operatives fit the definition. So do terminations premised on baseless conspiracy theories like the witch hunt around the mythical “censorship-industrial complex.”

The definition matters, because not everything will clear the bar. Some of the administration’s structural and personnel decisions might evoke outrage from its opponents but still be legitimate. Others may be legitimate but implemented with violations of process. Drawing the line will not be easy.

Transparency will ease the task. A timeline of personnel actions and structural changes, lists of individuals affected, and an inventory of decision-makers are all needed. One of the more difficult calls will be to decide where responsibility lies among career officials. A low-level employee in human resources who processed a wrongful termination can hardly be held responsible. The same does not hold true for a member of the Senior Executive Service who signed off on a decision, knowing it was made on false pretenses.

It will not be possible to make everyone whole. If someone was wrongfully terminated then replaced by a qualified person, it would hardly be fair to dismiss the civil servant hired as a replacement. Retaliation against career civil servants who “collaborated” with political appointees to purge undesirable employees under a previous administration could set off a never-ending cycle of retribution. Many structural changes will be politically challenging, if not impossible, to undo.

I never lied to Congress. I did explain truthfully that my office did not delve into domestic media outlets, as the transcript makes quite clear. My colleagues and I did not censor American citizens. Our actual work was to expose Russian cognitive warfare, which we did again and again and again . We also disrupted jihadist recruitment and countered Chinese propaganda.

We did not deserve to be smeared or pushed out of government, and our country is no safer or freer for what this administration did to us.

The center I helped lead began as a bipartisan initiative in 2016. Its employees shared a conviction that our enemies abroad are a greater threat than our political opponents at home.

That sentiment should be familiar to anyone who has worked in national security. I know many Republicans and Democrats who want to restore it as a guiding principle. Bipartisanship may seem unlikely today, but as political dynamics shift, a rigorous effort to expose the falsehoods behind the purges could start to repair the damage they did and help to prevent their recurrence.

Daniel Kimmage is former acting coordinator and deputy coordinator for the Global Engagement Center at the Department of State.
