articles.title: Real winner of Xi summit revealed as Trump looks to usher in new era with China
articles.summary: Trump's red-carpet welcome for Xi Jinping yielded fentanyl and tariff progress, but critical minerals, cyber threats and Taiwan remain unresolved.
articles.body: For years, being "soft" on China was a political insult hurled across the aisle. Great-power competition ruled. Washington increasingly prepared for the possibility of war with Beijing as the national security world pivoted toward the Indo-Pacific. The scene in D.C. last week looked markedly different as President Donald Trump attempts to welcome in a new era with the world's second-biggest superpower and growing adversary — especially when it comes to the ever-changing tech landscape. Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping with a red carpet and the pomp of a state visit last week, speaking warmly about his relationship with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) leader as the two sides looked for new areas of cooperation. "The summit went great — for Xi Jinping," Scott Kennedy, a China economics expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. 'RED CARPET FOR A DESPOT': TRUMP'S LAVISH XI WELCOME COLLIDES WITH GOP ANTI-COMMUNISM MESSAGE The reception was striking given how Washington's leaders have spent years describing the challenge posed by Beijing: Chinese hackers penetrating American networks, state-backed efforts to steal U.S. technology and trade secrets, unfair trade practices and a rapidly expanding military with its sights set on Taiwan. Gordon Chang, a China analyst and author who has long advocated a harder line toward Beijing, said there was a distinction between keeping lines of communication open with a rival and giving Xi the reception he received in Washington. "I understand that you have a need for dialogue, but when you have that dialogue, you don't necessarily have to have all of the ceremony and all the legitimization," Chang told Fox News Digital. "We can talk to the Chinese, but we don't need to do it in the way that occurred last week." Trump, however, is betting that a warmer relationship with Xi can produce results despite those enduring disputes. The question is how much Beijing's behavior has actually changed — and what Washington is willing to live with in pursuit of a more stable relationship. Kennedy explained that "the U.S. got a few small things — agreement to lower tariffs on $60B worth of goods, some purchases of specific items (such as agricultural and coal), the standing up of an AI dialogue, and alignment on major goals with regard to Iran and the Strait of Hormuz." "But Xi came away the winner because the current commercial ceasefire works mainly to Beijing’s advantage," he added. "It gives them time to continue unabated their drive for tech self-reliance, narrow the lead in various sectors, including AI, and maintain an imbalanced commercial relationship with its trading partners." TRUMP'S QUIET CHINA WINS ARE MORE IMPORTANT THAN XI'S EMPTY STATE VISIT Chang identified the same commodity as particularly valuable to Beijing: time. "While we talk, we defer taking action," Chang said. "So China got delay. And that is, I think, absolutely critical." The administration has gotten movement from Beijing on some long-running disputes. China has tightened controls on chemicals used to make fentanyl and, according to the White House, arrested 21 Chinese nationals in August based on information supplied by U.S. law enforcement. Trump is still pressing Xi to permanently restrict additional precursor chemicals, but the steps mark tangible progress on an issue that has bedeviled Washington for years. Trade is more complicated. Trump and Xi emerged from last week's talks with a new list of $30 billion in American products and $30 billion in Chinese products recommended for lower tariffs. For U.S. exporters, that could mean better access to the Chinese market for agricultural products, seafood, timber, cosmetics and medical devices. But there is a gap between the announcement and its impact. The two countries have agreed to consider favorable tariff treatment for the products — they have not yet put all of those lower tariffs into effect. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD And Washington is still trying to get Beijing to make good on commitments it already made. Nowhere is that more consequential than critical minerals, where China's dominance over global supply chains gives it enormous leverage over industries ranging from automobiles to weapons production. After his May summit with Xi, Trump announced that China had agreed to address U.S. concerns over shortages of rare earths and other critical minerals. Four months later, the issue remains unresolved. The White House said after last week's summit that Washington and Beijing "continue to work" on restoring adequate shipments. No new comprehensive critical-minerals agreement was announced. "China has not been living up to its commitments on supplying those minerals," Chang said. The gap between Washington's warmer posture and its longstanding concerns about Beijing extends beyond trade. Ahead of Xi's visit, Trump was asked about Chinese spying and cyber activity — an issue U.S. officials have spent years describing as one of the most persistent threats from Beijing. "When they say China spies on us, I say you’re right, and we spy on them too," Trump said. "They basically do what we do." Trump's own intelligence community describes the threat in markedly different terms. The intelligence community's 2026 Annual Threat Assessment calls China the "most active and persistent cyber threat" to U.S. government, private-sector and critical infrastructure networks. U.S. officials have accused Beijing-linked hackers of burrowing into telecommunications networks through the Salt Typhoon campaign and pre-positioning inside critical infrastructure through Volt Typhoon — activity officials have warned could give China the ability to disrupt communications, energy, transportation and water systems in a future crisis. "Yes, we do spy on each other, but there's a difference in the spying world," Chang said. "There are so-called legitimate targets. That's the governments of each state, defense contractors. What is not considered legitimate is spying on civilian institutions, NGOs, universities, all the rest of it. China does that. "I don't think it's his job to make excuses for China. His job is to protect the United States." Taiwan offers another test of the new relationship. A roughly $14 billion weapons package for the self-governed island remains in limbo months after Trump described it as a "very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. China claims Taiwan as its territory and has continued military activity around the island even as relations with Washington have warmed. "My sense is that Taiwan is nervous," Chang said, pointing to the still-pending package. "We still have not had that package green lighted." Trump has also looked to Xi for help beyond the Indo-Pacific. U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue said Trump warned Xi against Chinese intelligence, components or military assistance reaching Tehran amid the war with Iran and suggested Beijing subsequently took action, saying, "They pulled some things down." Perdue did not publicly specify what China curtailed. The emerging relationship, then, is not simply a story of rapprochement. It is a test of Trump's wager that engagement with Xi can produce concrete results while managing threats that Washington still considers serious. So far, that record is mixed. Beijing has taken steps on fentanyl, and the two countries are exploring lower tariffs on billions of dollars in goods. But China's critical-minerals commitments remain unresolved. Its cyber operations remain a top U.S. intelligence concern. U.S. defense strategy remains heavily focused on deterring China in the Indo-Pacific, and Taiwan remains one of the most dangerous potential flashpoints between the two powers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What has changed most dramatically, at least so far, is the relationship at the top — and Trump's willingness to bet that engagement with Xi can manage those risks better than confrontation alone.

articles.title: Jack Smith stresses strength of Trump cases, says he will not be ‘silenced’ by threats
articles.summary: Former special counsel Jack Smith stressed in prepared remarks that it was the evidence tied to President Trump’s own actions that prompted him to bring charges against Trump. The opening statement, obtained by The Hill, is to be delivered as Smith appears Tuesday before the Senate Judiciary Committee for his second appearance before Congress about…
articles.body:
Former special counsel Jack Smith stressed in prepared remarks that it was the evidence tied to President Trump’s own actions that prompted him to bring charges against Trump.

The opening statement, obtained by The Hill, is to be delivered as Smith appears Tuesday before the Senate Judiciary Committee for his second appearance before Congress about his investigations into Trump.

“The charges against President Trump were the result of the evidence,” the ex-federal prosecutor wrote. “Grand juries in two separate districts reached this conclusion based on his actions, as alleged in the indictments they returned.”

Smith is slated to tell the committee about the charges related to both the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case and the case tied to the president’s role in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

“I stand by my decisions as Special Counsel, including my decision to bring charges against President Trump. I made these decisions without regard to President Trump’s political association, activities, beliefs, or candidacy in the 2024 presidential election,” the opening statement reads.

“Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in criminal activity,” it continued. “If asked whether to prosecute a former President based on the same facts today, I would do so regardless of whether that President was a Republican or a Democrat.”

Smith in his prepared remarks also directly addressed Trump and criticized the erosion of prosecutorial norms under the president.

“I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the President or others,” he wrote, referencing “the vilification of the career prosecutors, FBI agents, and support staff who served on my team.”

“It is my belief that the rule of law faces challenges unlike any we have experienced in our lifetime. Individuals are threatened with criminal investigation because they are perceived to have opposed the President,” the former special counsel wrote. “Predetermined outcomes increasingly seem to take precedence over the Justice Department’s long-standing core values, traditions, and norms.”

In appearing before the panel, Smith will sit across from one of the most vocal critics of his investigation, Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), who has said the prosecutor was overzealous in subpoenaing the toll records of GOP lawmakers who spoke with Trump that day and the records of various conservative groups.

Smith’s statement does not address that criticism, but in the past, he has stressed that he obtained only call logs and did not have access to the content of the conversations. Some records were also obtained because the White House is tasked with preserving records through the National Archives, including contact with lawmakers.

The prosecutor did, however, argue that his actions were not politically motivated .

“My service has spanned both Republican and Democratic administrations. I am not a politician, and I have no partisan loyalties,” he continued in the statement. “My career has been dedicated to serving our country by upholding the rule of law and the core principles on which our country was founded.”

“I believe that there is no role for politics in the proper administration of justice. A prosecutor’s decisions must be based on the facts and the law,” Smith states.

Smith, who served under former President Biden, is largely unable to answer questions about the Mar-a-Lago documents case, which was brought after Trump repeatedly refused entreaties to return records slated to be archived from his administration — with Trump even ordering boxes moved to hide the papers from both his lawyers and law enforcement. A subsequent search of the home found more than 300 documents that had been marked classified, prompting Espionage Act charges.

The jurist overseeing the matter, U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, has shielded the release of Smith’s report discussing that case.

Questions are expected to primarily focus on Smith’s oversight of the Jan. 6 case.

Smith offered his view of the case in his prepared statement.

“Rather than accept his defeat in the 2020 presidential election, President Trump engaged in a criminal scheme to overturn the results and prevent the lawful transfer of power,” he wrote.

“The evidence showed that President Trump attempted to induce state officials to ignore true vote counts; to manufacture fraudulent slates of presidential electors in seven states that he had lost; to force his own Vice President to act in contravention of his oath and to instead advance President Trump’s personal interests; and, on January 6, 2021, to direct an angry mob to the United States Capitol to obstruct the congressional certification of the presidential election and then exploit the rioters’ violence to further delay it,” the prosecutor adds.

After Trump won the 2024 presidential election, Smith moved to drop the cases , citing Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting president.

articles.title: Trust nurses, not unproven AI tools
articles.summary: Nurses have been the most trusted profession in the U.S. for 24 years running, and with good reason: We care about you, we fight for you, and we don’t lie. We can’t say the same about those who attack our nurses union for protesting the artificial intelligence data company Palantir. It is no secret that…
articles.body:
Nurses have been the most trusted profession in the U.S. for 24 years running, and with good reason: We care about you, we fight for you, and we don’t lie.

We can’t say the same about those who attack our nurses union for protesting the artificial intelligence data company Palantir. It is no secret that Palantir helps federal agents target immigrants for deportation, helps the Israeli government kill Palestinians in Gaza, and helps our employers maximize profits by analyzing massive amounts of health care data.

The author presents a puppies-and-rainbows view of artificial intelligence deployed in any number of industries, including health care. But he is not a working bedside nurse. He is not a longshoreman. He is not a civil servant. He has no direct on-the-job experience with these products.

When you talk to people like us, the ones actually doing the real work that keeps our country running day in and day out, you will learn that AI is always for the benefit of the corporation’s profits, never to help us in our jobs. In our industry, hospitals have introduced AI to displace and replace nurses, to dangerously short-staff our shifts, to deny patients care, or to maximize billing — not to support our mission to save patients’ lives.

At Montefiore hospital in New York City, management in July laid off 12 veteran registered nurses who review patient charts and deal with insurance companies over coverage problems. It replaced them with A.I.-powered software.

At HCA hospitals across the country, the largest for-profit chain in the U.S., nurses are compelled to download and use a scheduler app called Timpani, a Palantir product. Timpani has wreaked havoc with their calendars and — no surprise — invariably fails to schedule enough experienced nurses on any given shift for the number and severity of patients.

Almost half of U.S. hospitals are using the electronic health record platform EPIC, which recently announced it had integrated ChatGPT into its system. Our nurses have already documented a whole host of systemic, unresolved problems with EPIC and fear that feeding patients’ personal medical data into ChatGPT is not only a gross violation of our privacy, but is just flat-out unsafe.

The companies boast that the system can generate automated end-of-shift hand-off reports that eliminate the need to talk to each other about patients. But any good RN knows that getting a verbal update on a patient from the previous nurse can mean the difference between life and death.

So don’t fall for people selling you a utopian view of AI. Nurses are not against technology, but we know the difference between technology that helps us take better care of you and technology that kills you.

All of the AI technology our employers are rolling out in our workplaces is untested, unproven, unregulated, and ultimately benefits their profit margin, not you or us. AI companies are essentially using patients and nurses as guinea pigs. We say no way. Trust nurses, not AI.

Jamie Brown, RN, is president of National Nurses United.

articles.title: Conservatives left grumbling after Trump’s welcome to Xi
articles.summary: President Trump’s warm embrace of Chinese President Xi Jinping last week has ruffled feathers in many corners of the GOP. Trump rolled out the literal red carpet for Xi, whose government has been accused of aiding Iran’s economy and military, in addition to decades of human rights violations and dictatorial rule. Republicans in Congress and…
articles.body:
President Trump ’s warm embrace of Chinese President Xi Jinping last week has ruffled feathers in many corners of the GOP.

Trump rolled out the literal red carpet for Xi, whose government has been accused of aiding Iran’s economy and military, in addition to decades of human rights violations and dictatorial rule. Republicans in Congress and in Trump’s orbit, including MAGA-world figures like Laura Loomer , were vocal with their criticism of the state visit.

“We have midterm elections in less than 2 months and so many people who say they are anti-communism sure enjoyed taking selfies in the presence of Xi with their glitz and glam,” Loomer wrote on social platform X .

Although there are plenty of issues that animate different factions of the right about U.S.-China relations, it wasn’t a policy disagreement, for the most part, as much as resistance to the cushy diplomacy Trump displayed in welcoming the Chinese leader. Red carpet aside, that included a state dinner and a military flyover, as well as a visit to the National Archives to view the Constitution and Declaration of Independence.

“They were complaining over style,” said William Chou , a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute. “They were not complaining over substance, just because I think there wasn’t that much substance, there were no major deliverables that came out of the meeting.”

Several Republican members of Congress, including some who are not usually quick to criticize Trump, went public with their displeasure over the president’s treatment of Xi. Their views were especially shaped by a closed-door briefing last week, where administration officials told senators that China is likely deepening its military cooperation with Iran.

“Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party,” Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) , chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said in a floor speech before the summit.

The House Select Committee on China released a video shortly before the visit showing images of Xi, telling viewers that he is “the biggest opponent of freedom and liberty in the world” and “the #1 adversary of the American people and our national security.”

Lawmakers and others had a slew of issues they hoped Trump would bring up with Xi, including export controls, agricultural purchasing, artificial intelligence, Taiwan and the treatment of political prisoners. But it’s not clear which, if any, of those came up throughout the three-day summit.

Chou said the lack of substance isn’t surprising, as such summits are typically a chance for photo-ops while working-level diplomats hash out policy. Plus, Chou said, neither side has “much desire to rock the boat right now” with the American midterm elections coming up and two more international forums involving both nations still to come this calendar year.

Dan Blumenthal, co-director of the Coalition Defense of Taiwan project at the American Enterprise Institute, said in an article published Monday that Trump’s treatment of Xi “as an equal” was very good optics for Xi but bad for Trump and the U.S. He called for Trump to use more economic leverage over China in the coming months but suggested that’s not likely to happen.

“Trump and Xi are already scheduled to meet twice more this year—at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November and the G20 summit in December—and there are indications that the US is ‘hollowing out’ the G20 agenda to turn the summit into a backdrop for another Trump–Xi meeting,” Blumenthal wrote. “For Xi’s part, he is happy to continue strutting down the red carpet so long as Trump is happy to continue rolling it out for him.”

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

This week marks 50 years since the first enactment of the Hyde Amendment, a piece of federal policy on annual government spending bills that prohibits federal funds from covering any abortion, with an exception for procedures that would save the life of the pregnant woman. The spending bill on which the first iteration of Hyde was attached became law on Sept. 30, 1976.

Anti-abortion groups are commemorating that anniversary, and Hyde’s endurance, with a rally at the Capitol steps Wednesday. The goal of the rally is to trumpet it as one of the most significant legislative achievements in the history of the anti-abortion movement and to urge Congress to hold fast on funding the government through regular order, full-year spending bills that keep Hyde intact.

“It has become consensus, or somewhat settled law, but it always does take a lot of work to keep it in there,” said Hannah Lape , legislative strategist at Concerned Women for America. “If we do lose the majority, the concern would be that either that the House would exclude Hyde or other members of the Hyde family of amendments from appropriations bills, and that would be something that we would have to go to bat for.”

Gavin Oxley , spokesperson for Americans United for Life, the group leading the rally, said there’s interest in “flexibility” on Hyde from both parties, which he said is “a losing strategy.”

“The Hyde Amendment has been the immovable red line of federal pro-life strategy for half a century, and it continues to serve as the backbone for defunding efforts that expand beyond direct subsidization of abortion,” Oxley said. “Popular opinion has been behind Hyde for 50 years, but politicians on both sides of the aisle seem to believe that abandoning public sentiment is good political strategy.”

The concern that lawmakers might compromise Hyde is not unfounded even with a Republican trifecta in power. Trump in January made waves when he suggested that House Republicans put aside their concerns about adding Hyde restrictions before extending or reforming expiring Affordable Care Act subsidies.

“Now, you have to be a little flexible on Hyde,” Trump told the lawmakers.

That comment sparked swift criticism from anti-abortion groups. Since then, Trump has nominated some allies of the movement to key Cabinet posts, including Todd Blanche as attorney general and Heidi Overton as Food and Drug Administration chief.

Some groups have gradually come back on board, but there’s still concern about whether the Trump administration will be aggressive enough on cutting ties between the federal government and Planned Parenthood or banning the mailing of mifepristone.

Concerned Women for America is also launching its regular election-year bus tour to encourage women to vote in the midterm elections, called “She Prays She Votes” and featuring a big pink bus. The tour will stop for rallies throughout October in Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia. More here .

American Compass published the first issue of its new online magazine, Commonplace. The magazine is intended to bring together essays from the right of center coalition and “be a home for development and advancement of its ideas and coalition.” The first edition includes pieces on conservative climate policy (by Chris Barnard), AI catastrophism (by Oren Cass) and much more. Read it here .

The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights released a report on the federal response to antisemitism on college campuses, the result of a bipartisan investigation into how the federal government and nine universities handled student protests, academic freedom issues, discrimination and vandalism, and other incidents in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel. The commission highlighted inconsistent responses from the institutions and called for increased capacity and transparency from federal agencies. Read the report .

articles.title: Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's removal from flat
articles.summary: The ban is part of a number of proposals that must be approved in parliament within 30 days.
articles.body:
Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last week.

Ministers met on Tuesday to discuss the proposals, which include a ban on evictions until 2030.

Announcing the measures, Health Minister Mónica García said they would bring relief to more than five million people - but opposition politician Míriam Nogueras said the agreement left "small landlords out in the cold".

The proposals - which have been presented in the form of two decrees - come into effect immediately, but must be approved by Congress within a month, although the government hopes to hold the vote as soon as this Friday.

Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government lacks a majority in parliament and has struggled to get right-leaning parties to approve previous decrees.

In April, a decree seeking to roll over rental contracts was blocked by right-leaning parties.

García, of the Sumar alliance, said other measures agreed upon on Tuesday included the rolling over of contracts until 2028; stricter regulation of short-term and room rentals; and banning the purchase of housing by investment firms.

"It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," García said.

Referencing the protests, she added: "Thanks to the mobilisations and the encampments. Without you, this would not have been possible."

But Nogueras, spokeswoman for the centre-right Catalan nationalists of Junts party, said: "We all agreed that evictions - where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros - obviously need to be stopped.

"Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property - putting them all in the same basket - is a mistake," she told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.

The minority government, which is made up of the Sánchez's ruling Socialists and junior partner the Sumar alliance, has 30 days from the decrees' publication to reach an agreement in parliament.

Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez urged political parties to support the decrees after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week.

"Congress has the opportunity to tell Maricarmen that her suffering was worth it... and that many people will benefit from her battle", she said.

But Valeria Racu, a spokeswoman for the Madrid Tenants' Union, said the battle had "only just begun", and called for more protests across Spain next weekend.

"We all have our eyes on the text, on the small print, to make sure this is the Maricarmen decree," added Alicia del Río, another spokeswoman for the organisation.

The two decrees approved by the cabinet contain enough to at least suggest that the government has been listening carefully to the demands of the activists who have been protesting in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere in recent days.

The temporary ban on evictions, the rolling over of rental contracts and the ban on investment firms - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property are all the kinds of policies that have been discussed by housing activists in recent days.

Pablo Bustinduy, minister of social rights, described the measures approved by the cabinet as "a first step towards the economic and social transformation of the country".

Bustinduy and his Sumar alliance had entered the negotiations with Sánchez's Socialists determined to take a stand on this issue, which is one they feel strongly about.

Sumar's tough stance was a major reason why talks between the coalition partners on the decrees went down to the wire ahead of Tuesday's cabinet meeting.

While the relatively bold new measures may please many on the left, they have raised the hackles of the Junts, whose support is again likely to be needed to approve them.

Junts and other parties on the right tend to be reluctant to intervene in the housing market, particularly if it means tipping the balance of the law in favour of tenants and against landlords, many of who are their natural electorate.

The question now is whether the social momentum generated by the Maricarmen Abascal case will override such reservations and manage to ensure this package of measures becomes law.

The hard men removing squatters in Spain

'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic

Ahead of the government's announcement on Tuesday, the lawyer for Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing crisis, said she would be allowed to return to her home after reaching a deal with the company that owns it on Monday.

Abascal, who was admitted to hospital after being forcibly removed from the apartment on a stretcher, was unable to attend the meeting and is yet to sign the deal.

Abascal's father first rented the flat in 1956 and she had continued to live in it after her parents died, with a cap on the rent, until investment company Urbagestión bought the property in 2018.

It raised the monthly rent to more than her monthly pension, leaving her unable to pay it.

In the north-eastern city of Zaragoza, another woman's eviction was temporarily suspended on Tuesday, the European Pressphoto Agency reported.

Esmeralda Tejero, 51, has lived in a flat in the city for eight years with her 11-year-old daughter, but stopped paying her rent some time ago as she could not afford it on top of her daily living costs, she told Catalan newspaper el Periódico on Monday.

Protests calling for housing relief measures broke out last week in Madrid and have spread to other cities including Barcelona, Seville, Malaga and Cadiz.

Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday demanding stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.

Hundreds of tents have been set up in the famous public square of Puerta del Sol since.

The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.

The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.

It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

articles.title: Trump touts Senate passage of Protect College Sports Act: ‘Really big deal’
articles.summary: President Trump late on Monday lauded the passage of the Protect College Sports Act in the Senate, calling the bill that looks to reshape college sports a “really big deal.” Lawmakers passed the bill in a 77-22 vote with bipartisan support after months of debate and pushback, including from critics of the NCAA. “This is…
articles.body:
President Trump late on Monday lauded the passage of the Protect College Sports Act in the Senate, calling the bill that looks to reshape college sports a “really big deal.”

Lawmakers passed the bill in a 77-22 vote with bipartisan support after months of debate and pushback, including from critics of the NCAA.

“This is a really big deal,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves. Congratulations to Randy Levine, President of the New York Yankees, and all of those who worked with him, on a job well done!”

Core priorities of the bill include providing the NCAA with sweeping federal antitrust protection to guard it from lawsuits over enforcing rules and placing a cap on how much money goes to student-athletes over their name, image and likeness. It would also guarantee scholarships for 10 years after eligibility and give athletes the chance to transfer once without sitting out for a year.

Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) co-sponsored the bill, along with Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.). The legislation includes most of the protections that the Student Athlete Fairness and Enforcement Act, co-sponsored by Cantwell, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), had when it was introduced last year.

Cruz said after the bill passed the upper chamber that college sports “were headed off a cliff.”

“Tonight, 77 Senators said enough,” the Texas Republican wrote on the social platform X . “The Protect College Sports Act passed with a massive bipartisan vote. It protects the athletes, protects the programs, and protects a great American tradition for our kids and grandkids. Now, it goes to the House. Let’s get this to President Trump’s desk before Election Day, on the set of College Gameday.”

Cantwell praised the bill’s passage, stating that the bill helps to “stop stealing money out of college [and] university institutions for education, for tuition, for professors and putting it into an arms race on sports.”

“It is putting a pin in the problems to stabilize the loss of women’s and Olympic [sports] and to create the opportunity to discuss the larger structure moving forward. That is why I think we have so much support,” she said in a press release .

The Southeastern Conference (SEC) and Big Ten endorsed the bill in July after initially not backing it. The Big Ten said it was “pleased” by the bill’s passage in the Senate in a short statement . The SEC called its passage “an important step forward establishing a clear and durable national framework for college athletes.”

The NAACP , the AFL-CIO and its sports council , and the Congressional Black Caucus all opposed the bill, raising concerns over pay equity, workers’ protections and who determines the future of Black athletes, coaches, agents and historically Black colleges and universities.

articles.title: Out of office but on the job: Work-cations are on the rise worldwide
articles.summary: A laptop glows in the pre-dawn light, balanced on a picnic blanket beside a child’s toy cup. Beyond the ridge, a bay opens like a postcard, and a calendar reminder pings for the first meeting of the day. Scenes like this sit at the heart of the “workation” trend, where work travels with people and the office becomes optional.
articles.body:
A laptop glows in the pre-dawn light, balanced on a picnic blanket beside a child’s toy cup. Beyond the ridge, a bay opens like a postcard, and a calendar reminder pings for the first meeting of the day.

Scenes like this sit at the heart of the “work-cation” trend, whereby work travels with people and the office becomes optional.

Managers already live this reality. Fresh CMI research reports that one in five managers has taken a work-cation. But only one in eight employers has a formal policy, causing a gap in uneven approvals and ad hoc expectations.

Momentum keeps building because employees see a personal payoff. A long-running YouGov poll found that 37 percent of people who can work remotely wanted a work-cation within the next 12 months, and travel brands now package the concept as a product. Leaders can turn that demand into a repeatable, safe, high-trust way of working.

Work-cations now sit inside mainstream talent conversations, and the numbers point to acceleration. A recent Grant Thornton study of 600 business leaders found that policies for international remote work rose from 59 percent in 2023 to 77 percent in 2025, signaling a quick shift from exception handling to standard process.

That shift mirrors a broader reordering of employee expectations. The Work In America survey reports that 92 percent of workers say psychological wellbeing matters when choosing an employer, and location flexibility increasingly acts as proof that leaders trust adults to deliver.

Interest skews young and ambitious. In the same YouGov poll , enthusiasm rises among people ages 18 to 34, and wider flexibility pressures keep building — survey evidence found 6 percent of employees left a job in the prior year due to limited flexibility.

Academic research frames this as a boundary change with staying power. A work-life blending review describes an emerging pattern where work and life threads weave together across the day, and University of Birmingham flexible work research tracks how technology reshapes time, travel and wellbeing for modern workers.

Workations succeed when leaders treat them as a governed form of flexible work, with clear eligibility and consistent approvals. CMI emphasizes that manager support grows when employers set transparent rules, highlighting the role of active management.

Manager capability becomes the multiplier for any workation scheme — pairing workation approvals with coaching on planning, feedback and outcome-based performance keeps standards consistent.

Start with operational clarity that fits the job. Define which roles qualify, the maximum length, core overlap hours, and service levels for customer response, then tie approvals to objective factors such as project timing and coverage.

Fairness comes from process and communication, especially in organizations with frontline roles tied to place. The Acas code of practice sets expectations for handling flexible working requests, and its approach maps well to work-cations through timely dialogue and consistent criteria. A hybrid working guide reinforces the value of an overall strategy so flexibility supports culture and inclusion.

Security deserves equal rigor because laptops travel through airports, cafes and shared networks. Technical controls support that human layer. A well-configured virtual private network and managed devices, paired with clear reporting channels for lost equipment, can keep risk within a range leaders can accept.

Cross-border compliance often becomes the hidden tripwire. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s remote work tax guidance signals a push for clarity as cross-border remote work spreads, and its Model Tax Convention update adds detail on permanent establishment questions, helping employers and advisers align on thresholds.

Work-cations deliver real value when they protect the human purpose that sparked the request in the first place. CMI respondents largely viewed the experience positively, often linking it to mental health and balance; leaders can reinforce that outcome by designing work-cations around sustainable energy and clear availability windows.

That starts with a philosophy of autonomy backed by humane expectations. The U.S. surgeon general’s workplace mental health framework urges leaders to build cultures that support connection, predictability and rest, which translates into simple norms like meeting-light afternoons and true off-hours during local evenings.

Vacation still matters, of course, even when a new setting feels restorative. Families push the model further, and their experience offers a practical signal for employers. Reports on worldschooling families show how travel, work and caregiving can blend into an intense routine, which makes planned downtime and local community even more important.

Executives who get this right treat a work-cation as structured flexibility, guided by policy and protected by culture. When leaders set clear rules, secure the work and defend genuine recovery time, work-cations become a retention tool that also raises manager confidence.

The laptop on the cliff then signals a modern organization that trusts its people and earns that trust in return. As policies spread, organizations that win talent treat work-cations as a disciplined practice, turning a popular request into a durable advantage that supports performance and loyalty across a distributed workforce.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

articles.title: Banned news outlets ask judge to extend block on White House enforcement
articles.summary: News outlets that sued to regain access to the White House after President Trump banned their reporters from the grounds are asking a federal judge to intervene in the administration’s ongoing efforts to keep CNN from covering the president via pool duty. In a new court filing this week, an attorney representing the outlets wrote…
articles.body:
News outlets that sued to regain access to the White House after President Trump banned their reporters from the grounds are asking a federal judge to intervene in the administration’s ongoing efforts to keep CNN from covering the president via pool duty.

In a new court filing this week, an attorney representing the outlets wrote that “the White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity.”

The Trump administration is enforcing the ban “unpredictably and inconsistently” and causing CNN “irreparable harm,” the outlets argued.

“Moreover, the ban independently violates the First Amendment by restricting access to and use of a nonpublic forum on viewpoint-discriminatory and unreasonable terms,” the media companies’ attorney wrote, reiterating an argument he made when the outlets initially sued to regain access to the White House.

The latest filing comes as the networks have decided to resume pool coverage while CNN’s ability to fulfill its duty in the rotating list of outlets covering the president’s daily activities remains in doubt.

Trump initially banned the outlets earlier this month, and when U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled last week that the White House violated the media companies’ due process rights, access for journalists working for the three outlets was restored.

Tensions flared between CNN and the White House again over the weekend when the outlet was kept from Air Force One as Trump traveled to Tennessee to attend a college football game.

The president has consistently accused CNN and other outlets of peddling “fake news” and suggested he has a right to keep them from covering him.

CNN is slated for pool coverage on Thursday. The Trump administration is required to submit a response to this week’s filing by Friday.

articles.title: O’Reilly not expecting Trump to return to ‘drain the swamp’ messaging
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly said Monday that President Trump will likely not bring back his “drain the swamp” message ahead of the midterms. O’Reilly, in an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance,” said he anticipates the president will argue that Democrats have “lost their way” before the election, as Republicans try to maintain control of Congress…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly said Monday that President Trump will likely not bring back his “ drain the swamp ” message ahead of the midterms .

O’Reilly, in an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance,” said he anticipates the president will argue that Democrats have “lost their way” before the election, as Republicans try to maintain control of Congress for the final two years of his term.

“I don’t think he’s going to go back, Donald Trump, to on the outside or, ‘I’ll drain the swamp.’ I think he’s going to look ahead and say, ‘I can do this for you if you let me complete the job.’ That’s what I think the theme will be,” the former Fox News host told host Leland Vittert.

Trump deployed the “drain the swamp” message frequently during his first presidential campaign, arguing at the time that a new era of politics was necessary.

With the midterms roughly a month away, Trump has urged voters to “pretend” as if he is on the ballot in a bid to drive turnout.

“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” the president said earlier this month at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas. “Just one more time, because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts.”

Trump and GOP lawmakers have also attacked Democrats as “communists,” as multiple democratic socialists have won primaries in deep-blue districts this year.

Decision Desk HQ , The Hill’s data partner, gives Democrats a 52 percent chance to take back the Senate and House.

A recent Emerson College Polling survey also found Democrats leading Republicans by 11 points on a generic congressional ballot.

O’Reilly said Monday that “more and more Americans are living in the moment” instead of “evaluating the big picture” of the economy.

He told Vittert, “They’re suffering because of gasoline prices and food prices and other things that are draining their money.”

Annual inflation was at 3.4 percent in August, as measured by the consumer price index. The national average price of a gallon of regular gas, meanwhile, is roughly $4.45 amid the Iran war , according to data from AAA .

articles.title: Bipartisan team in Congress looks to expand insurance coverage for ovarian cancer screening
articles.summary: A group of lawmakers spanning both parties and chambers is introducing legislation that would require insurance plans to cover genetic testing for patients with hereditary risk factors and expand education and outreach about gynecologic cancer risk. Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Katie Britt (R-Ala.) are leading the bill, the Ovarian Cancer IMPACT Act, which was…
articles.body:
A group of lawmakers spanning both parties and chambers is introducing legislation that would require insurance plans to cover genetic testing for patients with hereditary risk factors and expand education and outreach about gynecologic cancer risk .

Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Katie Britt (R-Ala.) are leading the bill, the Ovarian Cancer IMPACT Act, which was shared exclusively with The Hill. Their House counterparts on the legislation are Reps. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.).

Slotkin’s mother, Judith, died in 2011 from ovarian cancer. The senator mentions that, and the struggle her family had with insurance companies throughout her mother’s illness, as her motivation for running for office.

“No family should have to fight both a cancer diagnosis and their insurance company at the same time,” Slotkin told The Hill. “Women, especially in rural communities like Michigan, should be able to get the genetic testing and specialty care they need to catch this disease early or prevent it altogether. Our bill tackles this issue from every angle — awareness, outreach and access to care and testing — and I thank my colleagues from across the aisle as we all work to save lives.”

In addition to some provisions about insurance coverage of genetic screenings, the new bill includes reauthorization of a 20-year-old Centers for Disease Control and Prevention program, Johanna’s Law, that provides funding for a federal education campaign about gynecological cancers.

“I think far too many times in this body, we don’t stand up for the things that actually affect 50 percent of our population, which are women,” Britt told The Hill. “Making sure that both proper research dollars go to women’s issues, whether it is ovarian cancer, breast cancer, menopause, a number of things that affect women’s daily life or can change the trajectory of their life, is important and then also, like I said, making sure that that research and that technology … aren’t just there, but that hardworking people, the people from coast to coast, the people in rural Alabama, and people in urban areas all have access to those tools.”

The legislation is a rare alignment of Democrats and Republicans on expanding healthcare coverage and spending federal money on cancer prevention.

Slotkin, in a floor speech last year, criticized Republicans for attempting to cut healthcare and Affordable Care Act benefits.

“President Trump and my Republican colleagues are doing everything in their power to cut healthcare from average Americans, they’re just doing it in different and creative ways, because they know it’s politically unpopular to tell you to your face,” Slotkin said at the time.

articles.title: Ask your 2026 candidates where they stand on public health
articles.summary: Public health is now part of modern-day politics.
articles.body:
For decades, public health churned quietly in the background, an invisible shield that kept populations safe and minimized disease spread. Before the recent pandemic, most Americans knew little about the national, state or local public health structure.

During the recent 100-year COVID-19 pandemic , public health became front and center in America and caught the eyes of elected officials. Finding fault with public health actions during the pandemic, several states enacted new laws and measures to govern its operations and scope. Thus, like other campaign issues, public health is now part of modern-day politics .

Although public health and healthcare are different — public health focuses on keeping the community healthy, whereas healthcare focuses on individual health — they are intertwined. Considering the broad and important role of public health, and that changes in public health policy will affect community and individual health, we, the voters, need to know how our elected officials approach the related issues.

Below are a few — not all — of the positions we must consider from those entrusted to represent us.

First, there are community threats. What do your candidates believe are the biggest public health threats your community faces? What measures will they put in place to provide eyes and ears for what is happening in public health? When faced with new infectious disease threats, like the last pandemic, what is the strategy for containment or mitigation? Who will lead this response, and what will be your candidates’ role?

Next is food safety. Federal lawmakers are increasingly focusing on nutrition and Americans increasingly value the importance of nutrition. At the same time, we recently went through a national outbreak of cyclosporiasis that came from the food supply and sickened tens of thousands of people. What would your candidates do locally and nationally to help ensure food safety? If there is a food-related outbreak, how would they respond, and what type of resources would be needed?

Candidates should also address children’s mental health. Youth behavioral health was already in a difficult state when the pandemic hit and has worsened since. Some states have pulled back on collecting information about the mental and behavioral health of children.

What would your candidates do to assess children in our communities? What services are currently available in your community, and are they adequate? What types of programs would your candidates consider to address mental health needs in your community?

Discussion of vaccination requirements is essential. Our country is seeing declines in vaccination rates of children entering school. Some say it is their right to determine whether their child is vaccinated, citing personal choice, whereas others are supportive of vaccination requirements for school attendance.

Where do your candidates come down on this issue? Ask candidates if your region is experiencing outbreaks of serious, vaccine-preventable illnesses. What would be their response to an outbreak of measles or pertussis in the community where you live? What would be the role of the local Department of Health in managing this outbreak?

There’s also the impact of climate change. Climate change-related events are resulting in more wildfires , excessive heat exposure and increases in insect-borne illnesses . This impacts recreation in and outside of schools and affects overall individual health . What do your candidates perceive of the local and regional impact of climate change? What measures would they put in place to deal with this issue?

On healthcare, an individual’s ability to obtain medical care is often dependent upon their ability to obtain health insurance. Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act will result in some losing health insurance coverage. The recent elimination of 750,000 enrollees covered under the Affordable Care Act means that thousands will no longer have health insurance coverage. It is also well recognized that individuals without regular healthcare will have increased emergency room utilization at a time when such facilities are overburdened . What do your candidates propose to address this situation?

The delivery of healthcare and hospital sustainability in rural settings is another increasing challenge. Thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, rural hospitals will be under increasing financial pressure , and it is projected that many will close. The Rural Health Transformation Program has the potential to have an impact but will not compensate for related loss of hospital funding. It is also projected that up to 33 percent of rural hospitals will close in the near future. What state-level initiatives will your candidates champion to support struggling rural hospitals?

Finally, candidates should address policy development. Developing public health policies can be complex both in terms of scope and the information needed for their development. How will your candidates collect information related to public health policies? Which organizations will they work with? How will they balance information from leading medical organizations versus that from non-traditional medical organizations?

Now that public health is a visible part of American politics and of great importance to our individual and community well-being, we hope that those already elected and those running for office give public health the attention needed.

Scott A. Rivkees, MD, is a pediatrician. He is the former state surgeon general and secretary of Health of Florida.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Hegseth to double cuts to generals, admirals in major Pentagon shakeup
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth's State of the Force address doubles last year's cuts, targeting a 20% reduction in general and flag officer billets across all services.
articles.body: War Secretary Pete Hegseth will announce plans to reduce by 20% the number of positions reserved for generals and admirals during his State of the Force address on Wednesday. Hegseth approved reduction plans for the Army, Navy, Air Force and the military's joint pool earlier this month, according to memos seen by Fox News Digital. The services were directed to implement the plans and complete the reductions by Jan. 1, 2027. Wednesday's address in Quantico, Va. is expected to lay out Hegseth's priorities for the military in the year ahead, with the reduction in senior leadership positions among the changes he will unveil. The new target doubles the 10% overall reduction in general and flag officer positions Hegseth ordered last year as part of his effort to streamline the military's senior ranks. That earlier directive separately called for a 20% reduction in active-duty four-star positions and a 20% reduction in National Guard general officers. SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES MERIT-BASED MILITARY PROMOTIONS, TARGETS BIDEN-ERA DEI POLICIES Hegseth dubbed that effort "less generals, more GIs," arguing that reducing senior headquarters positions would push resources and authority toward troops closer to the fight. The latest reductions apply to billets — positions designated for generals and admirals — rather than an across-the-board removal of 20% of the officers currently serving in those ranks, a War Department source told Fox News Digital. At least some of the positions will be downgraded rather than eliminated altogether. In a Sept. 16 memo approving reductions to the military's joint pool, Hegseth directed officials to establish O-6 requirements for general and flag officer positions identified for downgrade, allowing colonels and Navy captains to fill those jobs. GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH The announcement comes exactly one year after Hegseth summoned hundreds of generals and admirals from around the world to Quantico, Virginia, for an extraordinary gathering where he laid out his expectations for the military's senior leaders and warned those who did not support his reforms to step aside. Hegseth has argued that reducing the number of generals and admirals would strip away unnecessary layers of bureaucracy and push authority down the chain of command. "This has been a deliberative process, working with the Joint Chiefs of Staff with one goal: maximizing strategic readiness and operational effectiveness by making prudent reductions in the general and flag officer ranks." Military commands have been asked to send top-performing service members who meet fitness and body-composition requirements and maintain "impeccable" grooming and uniform standards, according to published reports on internal Pentagon guidance for the event. articles.title: Big Oil can’t hide behind the Clean Air Act
articles.summary: The Clean Air Act was designed to shield Americans from harmful pollution. It was not designed to shield fossil fuel companies from legal accountability or to eviscerate states’ authority to protect their citizens from conduct that brings harm to communities and costs the taxpayers billions.
articles.body:
The first case that the Supreme Court will hear this term, Suncor v. Boulder , could have major consequences for state and local governments’ ability to protect their residents from tortious conduct by corporations that are knowingly putting profits over people.

In this case, the court can ensure that state and local governments from Maine to Hawaii can get a fair hearing in court to hold major oil and gas companies accountable for concealing and misrepresenting their decades-long knowledge that the unabated use of fossil fuel products would contribute to more destructive, more frequent and more extreme weather events.

Today, U.S. communities are facing billions of dollars in costs to protect residents from the onslaught of deadly fires, floods, droughts and extreme heat. The impacts from climate change are becoming increasingly prevalent and damaging, creating public health crises that threaten the lives and livelihoods of people all across our country — with the worst health impacts falling hardest on children and other vulnerable communities who can least protect themselves.

In Suncor v. Boulder, ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy are asking the justices to overturn a Colorado Supreme Court decision that allows one of those lawsuits, from the city and county of Boulder, to move forward. Though the Colorado courts soundly rejected their argument, the oil companies insist that they should not stand trial because their actions are somehow shielded under the federal Clean Air Act , the landmark law that was designed to limit air pollution and protect public health. As former senior EPA officials who spent years working to enforce the Clean Air Act, we can say with confidence that the oil companies’ arguments on this issue have no credibility whatsoever. As we explained in a brief joined by former EPA officials from both Republican and Democratic administrations, Exxon and Suncor can point to no language in the Clean Air Act that preempts Boulder’s claims. Why? Because there is none.

The city of Boulder is not seeking to regulate air pollution. It is only trying to recover monetary damages for local harms that the oil companies knowingly caused as they spewed both emissions that altered the climate and falsehoods about the consequences of such emissions.

These companies are alleged to have knowingly deceived the people of Boulder County by minimizing public health risks; as a result, the people of Boulder witnessed the destruction of 1,084 homes in the 2021 Marshall Fire and currently face extreme drought that threatens ecosystems and livelihoods. For Boulder County, the stakes in this case could not be higher.

While Boulder is explicitly not asking the court to regulate emissions or stop the production of fossil fuels, Exxon and Suncor have argued without evidence that a hypothetical ruling against them could disrupt the fossil fuel market. That argument is conjecture at best and fear-mongering at worst. It also rings hollow at a moment when the oil and gas industry is posting record profits while seeking to avoid accountability, thereby placing the burdens of their harmful practices squarely on the backs of America’s families.

Even the Supreme Court has doubts . The justices themselves have raised the question of whether they have jurisdiction to weigh in on Boulder’s claims before the Colorado courts issued a final judgment.

The people of Boulder deserve to get their day in court against the oil and gas companies that have brought direct harm to their communities. The purpose of the Clean Air Act has never been to protect fossil fuels over other energy sources or to shield fossil fuel producers from liability for deceptive business practices. State laws that prohibit corporations from misleading the public about the dangers of their products pose no obstacle to the Clean Air Act’s purpose of reducing air pollution to protect the public’s welfare.

The act empowers the federal government to set reasonable limits on carbon pollution emissions from motor vehicles, power plants, and oil and gas development, which together make up a whopping two-thirds of U.S. emissions . It does not prevent states from enforcing their own laws against companies simply because doing so may indirectly lead to a reduction in fossil fuel emissions. And in a staggering “have their cake and eat it too” move, while asserting that the Clean Air Act applies here, the current administration is doing everything it can to get the courts to say that the act does not in fact allow EPA to regulate greenhouse gases now or in the future. EPA did so just this month when it repealed the 2024 limits on carbon pollution from coal and gas-fired power plants. Similarly, some members of Congress who have filed a brief in support of Exxon and Suncor are pushing legislation to give oil companies an unprecedented and dangerous legal shield from cases just like Boulder’s. The fact that these members feel the need to introduce such a bill is in itself an admission that current federal law does not stand in the way of Boulder’s claims.

The Clean Air Act was designed to shield Americans from harmful pollution. It was not designed to shield fossil fuel companies from legal accountability or to eviscerate states’ authority to protect their citizens from conduct that brings harm to communities and costs the taxpayers billions. The Supreme Court should not block communities like Boulder from having their day in court.

Gina McCarthy is former White House climate adviser and administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Avi Garbow is former general counsel of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and founder of Fiery Run Environmental Strategies.

articles.title: GOP lawmakers challenge Trump’s nearly $1B funding clawback
articles.summary: Republican lawmakers are pushing back on President Trump’s decision to cancel nearly $1 billion in federal funding, setting up a new clash between the White House and members of Trump’s own party at a particularly precarious moment for the GOP. The administration announced Friday that it would use a budget maneuver known as a “pocket…
articles.body:
Republican lawmakers are pushing back on President Trump’s decision to cancel nearly $1 billion in federal funding, setting up a new clash between the White House and members of Trump’s own party at a particularly precarious moment for the GOP.

The administration announced Friday that it would use a budget maneuver known as a “pocket rescission” to claw back funding for a range of federal programs, especially grants through the Department of Health and Human Services that support minority students, refugee resettlement and children without legal status. The cancellation comes less than 45 days before the end of the fiscal year, meaning the canceled funds will be paused through the year’s end regardless of what Congress does in response.

The move threatens to further stiffen the government funding process, which is already mired in partisanship over how much the government should spend on defense versus domestic programs. Whether Congress can manage a regular funding procedure this winter is already in question and will be determined, in large part, by the outcome of the midterm elections.

The White House has defended the new cuts as necessary to eliminate government waste and fraud, arguing that some money originally intended for refugee resettlement is no longer needed because fewer people are crossing the southern border illegally.

But Republicans on the congressional Appropriations committees, who are supposed to be in charge of the government’s purse, have never liked rescissions. Several of them voiced concern that the White House is encroaching on Congress’s constitutional authority over federal spending.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, said in a statement Friday that the move is “the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse.”

“This move shows that OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law,” Collins said. “Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers. OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), asked whether he agrees with Collins that the move was unlawful, said he thinks “there’s that argument for sure.”

“I think as an appropriator, she feels strongly that these are decisions made by appropriators, and that the administration doesn’t have this authority. That again is something the courts probably decide,” Thune said. “You know, I think whether you agree in substance or not with what they did and argue that they, you know, be good stewards, and some of these things may be things that many of us agree with, but the process by which they did it is one that is going to be, I assume, subject to a lot of discussion and probably some litigation.”

Collins said she will work with her colleagues to fight the rescissions, telling reporters Monday that some options include inserting language in the next set of appropriations bills to prevent something similar from happening or taking legal action.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who is also on the committee, said while she thinks it’s possible to add more guardrails to funding in the next appropriations bills, Congress needs a more permanent fix to avoid further legal questions over federal funding authority.

She floated a long-term reform of the Impoundment Control Act, a 1974 law that’s supposed to prevent the president from freezing or reversing appropriated funds but in practice gives him more authority to do so through rescissions.

“I think we need more clarity to it,” Murkowski said of that law. “It’s something that when the OMB director first came in, he said he doesn’t think it’s constitutional. So we’ve got a debate lined up already between what he thinks he is able to do, and what we think he is able to do. So maybe we should clarify that confusion, probably not a bad idea.”

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), another appropriator, said the rescissions move was “wrong” and that it would hamper the regular government funding process, which is already at a partisan stalemate. He stressed that that process matters because Republicans and Trump want to boost defense spending through appropriations amid the war with Iran.

“To have OMB step in like this, I think is going to cause problems,” Rounds told reporters Monday. “We’re looking at a substantial increase being proposed for defense needs that we’ve got to get through, and it’s going to make it very hard for us to actually get an outcome in the next appropriations bill because if it was me and I make a deal on things that are important to me, and OMB has the ability just to decide they’ll only take part of the deal, it does not bode well for actually getting a fair appropriations process in the future.”

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), who is not an appropriator but has become more willing to critique the administration in his last term, said that “by law, the Administration must request rescissions through its Congress.”

“His team always push the norms. The Court will rule against and then he’ll bash the Supreme Court again,” Bacon said.

The Hill reached out to House GOP appropriators for comment.

Some conservatives, especially in the House, lauded Trump’s move, as they did with his attempts last year to cut spending on foreign aid, diversity programs and what they perceived as government “waste.”

“This is America First in action,” Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) said in a statement on Monday. “The Trump Administration is cutting wasteful spending that does not benefit American citizens. Hardworking taxpayers should not be forced to bankroll health and social services for people who broke our laws.”

The far-right House Freedom Caucus, in a post on social media, thanked Trump and OMB Director Russell Vought.

“Critics can cry all they want. The President is simply fulfilling his promise to cut waste — and he should keep going!” the caucus wrote.

articles.title: GOP pollster highlights ‘dangerous’ Trump midterm strategy
articles.summary: Republican pollster Frank Luntz on Monday called President Trump’s midterm strategy “dangerous,” with the GOP dealing with rocky political territory as Election Day nears. “There’s always been a historical advantage to the party out of power in the midterms, particularly in the first midterms, and we see that now, that there’s an energy challenge for…
articles.body:
Republican pollster Frank Luntz on Monday called President Trump’s midterm strategy “dangerous,” with the GOP dealing with rocky political territory as Election Day nears.

“There’s always been a historical advantage to the party out of power in the midterms, particularly in the first midterms, and we see that now, that there’s an energy challenge for GOP voters, and that’s what the president is trying to address,” Luntz told CNN’s Audie Cornish on “CNN This Morning,” referring to Trump’s repeated calls for Republicans to pretend that he’s on the ballot in November.

“Now, here’s the issue: When he is on the ballot, his people come out, they participate,” Luntz continued. “They did in the on-year elections, 2016 and 2024, and they did not in 2018, and they did not as much even when Joe Biden was the president … for the 2022 election, so that’s what he’s trying to do.”

However, Trump is facing an unpopularity crisis with the American public as the midterms inch closer. According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, the president’s approval rating was sitting at 38.3 percent on Tuesday morning, with his disapproval rating at 59.8 percent.

The president and his party are also dealing with issues like the unpopular Iran war, concerns about the cost of living and criticism of their immigration enforcement tactics.

“His numbers, his support is not as strong today as it has been in the past, so it’s a very dangerous strategy. But he needs his people to vote in a place like Texas,” Luntz said.

Earlier this month, during the Republican National Committee’s first midterm convention in Dallas, Trump told the crowd, “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot.”

“Just one more time, because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts. You’re going to lose your safety and security. You’re going to lose your wealth,” the president added.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Trump created an energy crisis — states can help fix it
articles.summary: More and more, states are proving grounds for responsible, forward-thinking energy policy — even when the federal government pulls back.
articles.body:
When President Trump retook office last year, the damage to the energy sector was immediate and relentless. Between legislation and executive orders, the administration has crippled federal agencies, jeopardized $14 billion in investments for clean energy and manufacturing, created chaos with tariffs and attacked energy relief programs .

Our organization — Third Way — has a climate and energy program that has fought back at the federal level. But we’ve also been convening governors’ offices and state agencies. Because more and more, states are proving grounds for responsible, forward-thinking energy policy — even when the federal government pulls back.

The need is urgent. This year, three-quarters of Americans have reported that their home energy costs have increased. Six months into the president’s war with Iran, gas and diesel prices have repeatedly hit record highs with no relief in sight.

In response, Trump has dismissed affordability concerns entirely . But states across the country that are trying to keep electricity affordable contend with rising demand from data centers, bringing innovative solutions to market and building more generation and transmission capacity.

States are transforming hollow promises for “ratepayer protection” into real policies that hold data centers accountable for the energy costs they impose. Arizona, Colorado, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Virginia are designing or have already implemented energy pricing rules to hold large power users accountable and ensure that residential customers are not subsidizing their costs.

In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) has even stepped in to stop rate increases while pushing for broader reforms. Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey (D), Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs (D), North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein (D) and Maine Gov. Janet Mills (D) have created expert task forces to tackle utility accountability , remove red tape for energy investment and develop strategies to prevent data centers from shifting costs onto ratepayers.

Good governance and improved project permitting are essential to easing the energy cost crisis. But as these states work through existing obstacles with the tools at hand, they’re also supporting innovative solutions and technologies to get the job done.

We’ve heard from many innovation champions, investors and businesses. They are eager to fill the vacuum left by the federal government’s retreat, especially when it addresses challenges faced by their governors’ offices and state legislatures. They are focused on expanding investment and creating jobs in future-focused energy industries.

Take North Carolina’s work on enhanced rock weathering , a nascent but promising agricultural practice that can boost crop yields and remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere . Recently, Third Way convened representatives from state agencies, Stein’s office, the mining sector, agribusiness, climate nongovernmental organizations and universities to discuss how enhanced rock weathering can benefit local businesses and farmers. North Carolina can serve as an example for other states trying to both engage local stakeholders and attract innovators.

States have stepped up during energy crises before. The Massachusetts Clean Energy Center and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority , for instance, were created in response to the oil shocks of the 1970s. Today, we’re facing global conflict, skyrocketing energy demand, increasingly unreliable infrastructure and a slipshod federal response. States are rising to the moment and keeping their energy economies humming.

They have a deep bench of expertise and talent, can prioritize local solutions and want regional cooperation. We’ve seen them convene utility representatives, project developers, labor groups, environmental nongovernmental organizations and state government officials to produce pragmatic and durable policies.

Americans cannot wait for congressional legislation or presidential action that may take years. Advocacy organizations like Third Way shouldn’t wait either. We should work with states to sharpen each other’s ideas and elevate impactful policies. Alongside combatting the Trump administration’s worst instincts and advocating for necessary policies, this effort can deliver for voters everywhere.

Jonathan Lane is the deputy director for Innovation, Francesca Hsie is deputy director for Electricity Third Way and Nicholas Yoon is a policy advisor for Innovation at Third Way .
