articles.title: GOP senator blocks move to prevent Trump from tearing down buildings honoring presidents
articles.summary: Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) late Monday blocked an attempt from Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) to prohibit President Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center. The bill Merkley attempted to pass under unanimous consent, which would have bypassed a floor vote if no one had objected, also had the support of Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska). Trump…
articles.body:
Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) late Monday blocked an attempt from Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) to prohibit President Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center.

The bill Merkley attempted to pass under unanimous consent, which would have bypassed a floor vote if no one had objected, also had the support of Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska).

Trump has threatened to tear down the performing arts center after a court blocked him from adding his name to Kennedy’s on its facade. The administration is also in court fighting a challenge to substantive renovations Trump wants to do, arguing that the building is “decrepit” and in need of a full remodel.

Merkley called for action on the Senate floor Monday night but was met with an objection from Lee. In a statement after the fact, Merkley said his bill would have prevented demolition of any national memorial to honor a U.S. president without an act of Congress.

“Trump’s threats are straight out of the authoritarian playbook and should infuriate every American who values our nation’s history and the rule of law,” Merkley said. “Instead of wasting taxpayer dollars putting Trump’s name on memorials and monuments as if he is a king, we should be focused on putting money back into the pockets of working families and honoring America’s greatest cultural institutions, not destroying them.”

Moments earlier, Lee also objected to a Merkley motion that would have blocked Trump from building a colossal marble arch between the Arlington Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) warned last week that Trump appears to be laying the groundwork for construction of the arch, despite a court order demanding prior notice before work begins.

articles.title: A political veto over NIH grants could leave East Palestine in the dark
articles.summary: The research that serves us is exactly the kind of work that could land on a veto list.
articles.body:
In February 2023, a Norfolk Southern train carrying vinyl chloride derailed in East Palestine, Ohio . Days later, officials vented and burned the chemicals, sending a black plume over our homes, our schools and our farms. I lived a mile away, raising my kids under a cloud of uncertainty.

Since then, my community has asked one question more than any other: What did this do to our bodies? Presidents and cabinet secretaries came. Cameras came. Most of them left.

The scientists stayed. They stayed because the National Institutes of Health funded them. Through the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences , researchers have spent years collecting blood, urine, air and soil samples from residents who volunteered their own bodies and homes as evidence.

One finding, published in Environmental Science & Technology , should stop anyone in their tracks. Our research team found HEMA, a breakdown product linked to vinyl chloride and related compounds, in the urine of 74 percent of East Palestine residents tested five months after the disaster. In a comparison group from Marietta, Ohio, they found it in none. Nationally, it shows up in about 5 percent of people.

That is what NIH funding buys: answers no one else would find. Now the White House wants to change how those dollars are awarded.

According to The New York Times , the Office of Management and Budget is drafting an executive order that would create an outside committee empowered to veto NIH grants that don’t fit the president’s political agenda. It grew out of a contentious Oval Office meeting where Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought accused NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya of funding work at odds with administration priorities. Bhattacharya has resisted.

For decades, NIH has picked projects the same way. Experts review the science and fund what is most likely to produce answers. A political committee would potentially ask a different question. Not “Is this good science?” but “Does this meet our agenda?”

That question should worry every community like mine. East Palestine is a small, conservative, working-class village. We are not an Ivy League campus, and we are not anyone’s culture war. But the research that serves us is exactly the kind of work that could land on a veto list.

Environmental health studies routinely produce findings inconvenient for powerful industries, including railroads. Research on how income, geography and occupation shape health outcomes is disparities research; a field already cut back under recent executive orders. Rural Appalachia lives inside those statistics as do many other marginalized communities across the nation.

A veto doesn’t have to be used often to do damage. Its existence is enough. Researchers planning the next decade of their careers will steer away from any study that might look political to someone at the Office of Management and Budget. Communities facing the next chemical disaster will find fewer scientists willing to show up.

And disasters keep happening. Derailments, industrial fires, wildfires and chemical spills happen every year, and each one leaves families asking what we asked. Some health effects take decades to appear. Children exposed today will not show certain outcomes until they are adults. Answering those questions requires following the same people for years. A grant that can be yanked midstream is a grant no one can plan around.

It also breaks trust, and trust is the hardest thing to rebuild. My neighbors did not hand over their blood and urine lightly. Many already felt abandoned by agencies that told them everything was fine. They participated, and continued to participate years later, because researchers promised to stay and to share what they found. If Washington can cancel that promise over the politics of a study, participants will stop believing any promise at all.

Congress has already shown it understands this. Lawmakers rejected the administration’s proposed cuts to biomedical research and blocked a rule injecting political review into federal grantmaking. That was the right call. But a temporary block won’t stop a permanent order.

Lawmakers should use this year’s appropriations bills to protect peer review in law, bar federal funds from supporting any body that can overrule expert review of NIH grants and protect awarded grants from political cancellation. This is not a partisan ask. Merit review has served Republican and Democratic administrations alike, and red counties just as well as blue ones.

East Palestine did not choose this disaster. We chose to help science answer it, for ourselves and for whoever is next. Which questions are worth asking is a judgment scientists spend careers learning to make. It is not one that a committee at the Office of Management and Budget is qualified to overrule.

Misti Allison is the Community Advisory Board chair of the East Palestine Train Derailment Health Research Program and founder of Disaster Voices Institute. She lives in East Palestine, Ohio.

articles.title: Hollywood actress upset her son isn't gay fumes in bizarre spectacle at Human Rights Campaign gala
articles.summary: Camryn Manheim told the Human Rights Campaign dinner she "always wanted a gay son," but her boy turned out straight despite her very best efforts.
articles.body: A Hollywood actress used her platform on stage at a far-left Human Rights Campaign (HRC) event to complain that despite her best efforts, her son turned out to be heterosexual. Camryn Manheim, best known for her role as Ellenor Frutt in the late 1990s and early 2000s drama series "The Practice," introduced and presented her friend and fellow actress Marcia Gay Harden with the Ally for Equality Award at the HRC's National Dinner on Sunday. "For Marcia, of course, this is deeply personal to her," said Manheim of this year's recipient of the prestigious award. "She has three remarkable children who all align with the LGBTQ+ community, which is another thing that deeply irritates me about her, because I always wanted a gay son." GLAAD RELEASES 'PARTICULARLY CONCERNING' REPORT SHOWING SHRINKING LGBTQ REPRESENTATION THIRD YEAR IN A ROW She then launched into a tirade about how her son is heterosexual. "I love that relationship between gay sons and their mothers," she said from the stage. "I wanted to be the picket sign-holding mom who would beat the s--- out of somebody for her kid. I mean, let's just admit it, gay sons are the best, right? Right!" "I have photographs of my son in high heels, in full drag, he knows every word to every musical ever written, his fairy godfather, Aaron Walton, is here with us tonight. I mean, truly, I thought I had this f---ing thing locked up, but no, no, he's the only straight guy in his entire musical theater company," Manheim complained. Manheim's only child, Milo Manheim, 25, is an actor best known for his starring role as Zed in the Disney Channel film franchise "Zombies." He played Joseph in the 2023 Christmas musical, "Journey to Bethlehem," and in 2018 came in second place on season 27 of "Dancing with the Stars." LOG CABIN REPUBLICANS REMOVES 'T' FROM LGBT ADVOCACY, SAYS 'RADICAL' TRANS ACTIVISTS ARE ERODING GAY SUPPORT Manheim, during her recorded remarks, relayed a story about Harden, a 2021 Oscar winner for best supporting actress in the 2000 film "Pollock," calling her a decade ago to tell her that her son was gay. "All I said was, 'Oh my God, you are so f---ing lucky!" Manheim said, yelling into the microphone and drawing a round of applause from the crowd. And about a week later, I was at Marcia's house for dinner when an Amazon package was delivered, and inside, I'm not kidding you, was a pair of thigh-high patent leather boots, like kinky boots," Manheim continued. "And I thought, 'oh come on, now she is just showing off!" DEMOCRATS TURN ON CONGRESSIONAL HOPEFUL AFTER 'HIDING' LGBTQ+ VIEWS FROM MUSLIM VOTERS HRC is America's largest civil rights group dedicated to "engaging and mobilizing millions of pro-equality voters and supporters to elect pro-equality leaders and to demand equity-based policies and legislation." The organization was founded in 1980 by gay rights lobbyist Steve Endean and today boasts 4 million members. Sunday night's dinner was part of the Human Rights Campaign's events program, which it says reaches more than 20,000 people each year through 30 fundraising dinner events. It allows the group to "elevate LGBTQ+ candidates around the country, keep volunteers engaged, amplify our work in the local community, and solicit corporate sponsorships and donations through our auctions." Online, reactions ranged from dismayed to disgusted. "How do any straight males survive mothers like this? It's a miracle some of them come out normal," said a right-wing commentator who goes by Peachy Keenan. "These people are mentally ill. They need to be institutionalized or thrown in prison for trying to groom children," said Andy Froemel. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It’s the entertainment industry mothers who are the psychos," online personality @shipwreckedcrew, who boasts more than 180,000 followers, said. "These people are sick," radio show host Joe Pagliarulo said. "Liberalism is a performative sickness," said Jon Nanjarian. Fox News Digital reached out to HRC and representatives for Manheim but did not hear back at time of publication.

articles.title: Trump launches America.gov, AI-powered government services hub

He thanked Joe Gebbia, the Airbnb co-founder who now leads the National Design Studio (NDS) and services…
articles.body:
President Trump launched a website Tuesday that uses artificial intelligence to help Americans navigate the federal government and find information and services.

Trump touted the website, America.gov, during an event at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington. He thanked Joe Gebbia, the Airbnb co-founder who now leads the National Design Studio (NDS) and services as the first-ever U.S. chief design officer, for being the “mastermind behind many of the incredible breakthroughs.”

“It’s the ultimate product. It’s called America when you think about it,” Trump said. “With America.gov, the federal government no longer stands in your way, and it stands only at your service. And that’s what we’re doing. We’re simplifying it. We’re glamorizing it. We’re making it what it should be.”

The website features a search bar that lets users ask questions about how to navigate certain services. It tells users that all answers provided come from official government websites and includes links to the original sources.

The president said this project has been in the works since the early days of his second administration.

“Instead of forcing citizens to search through the endless maze of tens of thousands of terrible government websites and rules, and more than 10,000 forms … you’ll now have one front door for every single question,” he said.

He said “in theory” the website cannot be hacked into.

“It’s built from the ground up with your privacy and security totally in mind,” Trump said. “To ensure that your personal information is not collected or stored, and your conversation disappears when you leave, and everything stays totally private.”

The website says that in early 2027, users will be able to complete forms, applications and renewals, like enrolling in Medicare and applying for a passport.

Trump also signed an executive order at the event directing federal government agencies to make their services integrate with the website.

The event included different people showing what can be done on the website. Several Cabinet and administration officials and tech leaders were also in attendance.

articles.title: US revokes Latin American officials’ visas
articles.summary: The Trump administration revoked visas from 27 Latin American officials, including Bolivia’s top prosecutor, former officials and their family members over allegations of corruption and ties to drug trafficking. The visa revocations targeted officials and their family members from Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, the State Department announced Monday. Earlier this month, Secretary of State…
articles.body:
The Trump administration revoked visas from 27 Latin American officials, including Bolivia’s top prosecutor, former officials and their family members over allegations of corruption and ties to drug trafficking.

The visa revocations targeted officials and their family members from Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, the State Department announced Monday.

Earlier this month , Secretary of State Marco Rubio pledged to combat drug and human trafficking following a visit to Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, whose right-wing leaders are notably aligned with President Trump’s tough stance on illicit drug trade.

The administration is also barring Bolivia’s attorney general, Roger Mariaca, and his family from entering the U.S., accusing him of accepting bribes to help drug traffickers and violent criminals avoid prosecution.

The State Department said it is “taking actions to fulfill the commitments to defend democratic governance across our hemisphere against corruption and narco-trafficking.”

“Under the Trump Administration, corrupt foreign officials can no longer freely enter the United States,” the department said in a statement .

Visas were revoked for 12 other Bolivians, including prosecutors, judges, a former justice minister and a police official. Nine Bolivians without current visas were made ineligible to receive them in the future.

Two Colombians, two Ecuadorians and a Peruvian judge were also targeted.

The move comes under a new visa policy aimed at foreign nationals accused of undermining democratically elected governments through corruption or facilitating drug trafficking.

“Undermining a democratically-elected government is a threat to security and rule of law in the Americas and will not be tolerated,” the department said. “This is a durable mechanism that allows the United States to act quickly, in coordination with our partners, as evidence develops.”

The restrictions are part of Trump’s “Shield of the Americas” initiative, which calls for participating countries to work together to combat drug trafficking, organized crime and corruption in the Western Hemisphere.

articles.title: With Trump’s help, the Senate looks good for Democrats
articles.summary: Democrats are projected to regain control of the Senate during the Nov. 3 elections, potentially flipping multiple Republican seats in states such as North Carolina, Ohio, Alaska, Maine, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
articles.body:
Last week, the National Republican Senatorial Committee tried to reassure its top donors, gathered on Georgia’s Sea Island, that everything looks rosy for the midterms. “I told attendees that I think all incumbent Republican senators will hold their seats because we have good candidates who are well funded,” pollster Erik Iverson told reporters .

But, as Axios scooped, Iverson was almost laughed out of the room. One participant called it “delusional.” Donors see the writing on the wall, and they know it doesn’t look good for Republicans.

The current Senate line-up is 53 Republicans and 45 Democrats plus two Independents, 53-47. This year, there are 35 Senate seats up on Nov. 3 , of which Republicans are defending 22, and Democrats, are defending 13.

At first, the 2026 Senate field favored Republicans. But that’s no longer the case. Latest forecasts by leading pollsters say just the opposite. According to fredcornell.com, Democrats have a 60 percent chance of regaining control of the Senate. RacetotheWH.com rates Democrats’ chance of success even higher, at 7 2 percent .

To take control of the Senate, Democrats need to retain the seats they now hold, plus pick up four more. On both fronts, they look strong.

Incumbent Democratic senators practically certain to be reelected include Delaware’s Chris Coons, New Jersey’s Cory Booker, Rhode Island’s Jack Reed, and Massachusetts’ Ed Markey. In Georgia, Jon Ossoff was once considered the most vulnerable incumbent Democrat, but his reelection campaign has proven so successful he’s already being talked about as presidential material in 2028.

After a bitterly-fought primary, it looked like Michigan Democrats might have a hard time holding onto the seat vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters, but candidate Abdul El-Sayed has united the Democratic Party behind him and leads in the polls against Republican Mike Rogers.

For a while, it looked like Democrats might have a hard time holding onto retiring Jeanne Shaheen’s Senate perch in New Hampshire, but latest polls give Democrat Chris Pappas an 8-point lead over Republican John Sununu .

What’s most impressive is how Democrats have turned the tide in red states and stand likely to flip several Republican seats. Starting in North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper is almost certain to become the Tarheel State’s next U.S. senator.

Four other currently Republican seats are definitely in play and look good for Democrats: Ohio, where, in most polls, former Sen. Sherrod Brown has a slight lead over Sen. Jon Husted (R); Alaska, with former Rep. Mary Peltola out in front of Sen. Dan Sullivan (R); Maine, where Sen. Susan Collins (R), facing the toughest fight of her political life, is deadlocked with Democrat Troy Jackson; and perhaps most stunning of all, a 5-point lead in Texas for Democrat James Talarico over Donald Trump’s anointed and admittedly flawed candidate, Republican Ken Paxton.

Surprisingly, two more possible red-state pickups have popped up on the Democrats’ screen. In Iowa, where Democrats haven’t won a U.S. Senate seat since 2008, two-time Paralympic gold medalist for Team USA Josh Turek, endorsed by President Obama, holds a small lead over Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, endorsed by President Trump. Deep-red Kansas is also suddenly in play, with the remarkably strong showing by pastor Adam Hamilton, founder of America’s largest United Methodist Church, now running ahead of GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. Kansas hasn’t sent a Democratic senator to Washington since 1932.

Then, last weekend, came the real shocker: news that Darline Graham, handpicked by President Trump to take the seat of her late brother Lindsey Graham in South Carolina, is in trouble — not only among Democrats, but also among Republicans angry over Trump’s endorsing her over longtime conservative, Freedom Caucus Rep. Ralph Norman. The latest poll by the Trafalgar Group, a GOP pollster, shows Graham with only a 1-point lead over Democratic challenger Annie Andrews in a state Donald Trump won in 2024 by 17.9 points.

Add ‘em up. That’s eight vulnerable Republicans, of whom Democrats need to unseat four. Which is no certainty, but certainly a possibility. Especially since Republican incumbents are forced to defend a president who broke his promises to cut prices, lower mortgage rates, end the war in Ukraine, and start no new wars — and now spends most of his time talking about the ballroom.

If Democrats recapture the Senate on Nov. 3, Donald Trump will have no one to blame but himself.

articles.title: Media freedom perceptions hit record low: Survey
articles.summary: A new poll found that Americans’ perceptions of media freedom hit a record low, reaching its lowest point since pollsters started asking the question almost 20 years ago. Gallup released a poll Tuesday showing that 69 percent of Americans believe there is a lot of media freedom in the U.S. The new figure is 6…
articles.body:
A new poll found that Americans’ perceptions of media freedom hit a record low, reaching its lowest point since pollsters started asking the question almost 20 years ago.

Gallup released a poll Tuesday showing that 69 percent of Americans believe there is a lot of media freedom in the U.S. The new figure is 6 points below where it was in 2025, which saw a 5-point increase between 78 percent in 2023 and 82 percent the following year.

The highest percentage of respondents to say the U.S. has a lot of press freedom was 89 percent, back when Gallup first asked the question to Americans in 2010.

Gallup revealed a widening partisan divide over the question of media freedom, with 91 percent of Republican respondents saying U.S. media has many freedoms. This is an 8-point rise since GOP respondents were asked in 2024, under former President Biden.

Among Democrats and independents, however, those numbers have lowered with 68 percent of independents and 57 percent of Democrats saying the media has many freedoms, both down from 75 percent and 68 percent in 2025, respectively.

Perceptions have also fallen below the median average among other Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries, which generally sits at around 80 percent. That median hit 75 percent in 2025, with 2026 marking the first year on record where the U.S. sat below the median, at 69 percent.

“Public belief in U.S. media freedom continues to erode, while trust in the news media remains on the low end of what Gallup has measured historically,” the pollster wrote. “Many Americans lack a shared perspective toward their news environment, given partisan divides in perceptions of media freedom and trust.”

Challenges to media freedom have made headlines in recent weeks after President Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters who cover the White House, accusing them of peddling “fake news.” The outlets responded with a lawsuit, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled last week that the White House violated the media companies’ due process rights.

Kelly restored their access, but White House officials barred CNN from boarding Air Force One as Trump traveled to Tennessee to attend a college football game.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday that the president had “every right” to block CNN’s reporters from joining the White House press pool on Air Force One. He added that reporting perceived by the administration as “complete misinformation” rises to the level of a “national security problem” for U.S. relations with other countries.

The Gallup survey was conducted from May 1 to June 10 and included 1,000 respondents. The margin of error is 4.1 percentage points.

articles.title: New York Times gaming engineer gunned down by in-laws in Califorinia, police say
articles.summary: A man is dead and his mother-in-law and father-in-law are behind bars after a daylight shooting in a parking lot across from a police station.
articles.body:
DUBLIN, Calif. ( KRON ) — A man is dead and his mother-in-law and father-in-law are behind bars after a daylight shooting in a California parking lot across from a police station.

The shooting occurred about 3 p.m. on Saturday in the parking lot of the Dublin Sports Grounds. A police officer reported that he was driving by the park when he spotted Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old Dublin resident, on the ground. Reports of the shooting to 911 began around the same time.

McKinsey was reported to be suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. He was later pronounced dead at the scene.

The Dublin PD arrested two suspects in connection with the shooting. They were identified as Shili Chen and Shouyang Zhang — McKinsey’s 76-year-old in-laws.

The shooting has left the community in shock.

“It’s just surprising here in Dublin, it’s a quiet community,” said Joshua Boothby, who works at the park.

On Monday, The New York Times confirmed to Nexstar’s KRON that McKinsey was head of engineering for games at the outlet and had been at the paper since January 2023.

The two suspects were arrested within minutes with the help of witnesses, police said.

Chen and Zhang were booked into Santa Rita Jail on first-degree murder charges. Jail records for the two also include charges of child abuse or endangerment. They are currently being held without bail and scheduled to be arraigned on Wednesday morning.

No motive in the shooting has yet been announced. Court documents obtained by KRON, however, indicate that McKinsey and his wife, Candice Jang, had each filed separate reports of domestic violence against one another.

articles.title: Nancy Guthrie investigators reviewing ‘new possible ransom note,’ sheriff’s department says
articles.summary: The department said investigators are also looking into social media comments about the note to determine its credibility.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) – Investigators in the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie , the 84-year-old mother of “Today” show host Savannah Guthrie, say they are reviewing a new possible ransom note.

The Pima County Sheriff’s Department released a statement late on Tuesday announcing that the joint police and FBI task force was “recently made aware of a new possible ransom note related to the Nancy Guthrie investigation.”

“Investigators are also aware of social media comments regarding the note and are looking further into the information to determine its credibility,” the statement said.

Content of possible new Nancy Guthrie ransom note unknown

The department did not say who received the note, what is says or when it was sent.

The sheriff’s department previously released the full text of two ransom notes sent to Tucson television station KOLD in hopes that someone would recognize the writer’s distinctive word choice and phrasing.

The first of those notes demanded bitcoin and included details about a white smartwatch and a destroyed floodlight that had not been made public.

The second claimed Guthrie died shortly after she was taken, according to the release.

No arrests made, months after disappearance

Nancy Guthrie was first reported missing on Feb. 1, and authorities believe she was taken from her home in the early hours of the morning.

Photos of an armed, masked suspect were recovered from a camera at the home, but no suspects have been publicly identified, and no arrests have been made.

Anyone with information is urged to contact the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI, 88-CRIME at 88crime.org or through the P3 Tips mobile app.

Apparent confusion over team names derailed a line of questioning as Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) grilled former special counsel Jack Smith on Tuesday about his attendance at a basketball game, suggesting the prosecutor may have coordinated with others bringing charges about President Trump.

The exchange would later prompt Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) to say the panel had been “witness to a narrative, a false narrative of accusing [Smith] of being at a game that you were nowhere near, and I suppose that was supposed to be in furtherance of some sort of conspiracy.”

Schmitt asked Smith if he had traveled to Atlanta in 2024 to watch an Atlanta Hawks basketball game, alluding to the trip as a chance to meet Fani Willis, the top prosecutor in the city. Willis also brought charges against Trump.

Schmitt said he had texts referencing the game, though a board displaying the messages was only briefly shown by the senator’s staff.

Schmitt seemed surprised when Smith said he did not recall going to Atlanta during that time period and also said he did not meet Willis. For his part, Smith seemed puzzled.

“I really don’t think so. It’s possible I flew through the Atlanta airport on the way to Florida, but I do not have a recollection of going to Atlanta. I definitely did not go to a Hawks game,” Smith said.

The significance of the trip from Schmitt’s perspective was that the February 2024 game he referenced was the day after Willis revealed she was in a relationship with one of her own staffers, sparking a firestorm of scrutiny around the already high-profile Fulton County election interference case.

“Let me just give you a little context. The day before Fannie Willis came clean with her affair with the prosecutor, you know, the Atlanta prosecutor that was also trying to get Trump. The next day, were you in Atlanta?” Schmitt asked.

Smith said he had at one point attended an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland, as he wanted to watch Caitlin Clark play.

Schmitt’s questioning ended with the lawmaker calling Smith a “villain” and “dirtbag.”

Amid protests from Democrats, Schmitt initially refused to again show the text messages he displayed on the board, prompting some to say Smith deserved to see what he was being asked to respond to. Schmitt later relented.

The text messages show one prosecutor on Smith’s team having booked a meeting room only to be told by another staffer that Smith is “already down here.” The text messages he displayed don’t reference any basketball team names or games, though Schmitt at one point told Smith, “I don’t think you know that we have this stuff.”

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), who was next in line for questioning, posited that Schmitt may have confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes.

“Could it then be that University of Iowa is the Hawkeyes? … That might be the confusion over the names of the team,” she said.

“That might be the confusion over the names of the team. But perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully.”

Schmitt then snapped that Klobuchar was trying to “rehabilitate the witness.”

After wrapping her questioning, Klobuchar criticized Schmitt for calling the prosecutor a “dirtbag.”

“We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. Iowa, the Iowa Hawkeyes, played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93 to 85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over 30 points, so it must have been a pretty good game. The game was, in fact, in Maryland, Mr. Smith,” she said.

“And I would just say, for a U.S. senator to have false information and imply, based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology.”

articles.title: Beijing blackout: Why we may never know what happened between Trump and Xi
articles.summary: The recent summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping was a win-win for China — at least, as far as anyone can tell.
articles.body:
The political, economic and security competition between China and the U.S. — the world’s two greatest economies and most powerful militaries — is nothing less than a titanic struggle. The fact that the U.S. is the leader of the free world and that China now dominates the modern “Axis of Evil” that includes Iran, North Korea and Russia makes it also an existential conflict for Western civilization — with the fate of Taiwan constituting the ultimate test case.

In that context, last week’s summit meeting between President Trump and Xi Jinping was a resoundingly anti-climactic dud, apparently accomplishing nothing to resolve either Taiwan’s future or the larger issue it symbolizes. Instead, a meeting with cosmic stakes became little more than an exercise in diplomatic reciprocity between a Chinese totalitarian and an aspiring would-be dictator, in thrall to Xi and almost all the world’s other tyrants (with the notable exception of their front-line proxy , the Islamic Republic of Iran).

Xi’s objectives for the U.S. summit were three-fold.

First, he wanted validation by the American president that China is an equal player in the international geopolitical game. Xi got that with a lavish White House reception that more than matched Xi’s welcoming ceremonies for Trump in May , and an unprecedented airport welcome by Trump.

Next, Xi sought a softening by Trump of U.S. support for Taiwan, and to disabuse Taiwan of any idea that the United States can accept Taiwan’s independence over the long term. Beijing’s ultimate aim is an explicit statement that Washington “opposes” that elevation of Taiwan’s status rather than the more neutral, non-committal “does not support” independence, which can be read as a disavowal of an active U.S. role but acquiescence in such a final outcome. Xi wants the door closed absolutely and permanently — and he wants America’s complicity in closing the door.

It is not yet known whether Trump agreed to the demand, because Xi clearly succeeded in his third objective for the meeting: that nothing occur publicly that would disrupt U.S.-China relations and the atmospherics of a cooperative Xi-Trump relationship. And if Trump did bend to Xi’s pressure on Taiwan, suppression of that fact would suit Trump’s purposes as well, given his weakened political position just before the midterm elections.

Neither Xi nor Trump would welcome aggressive questioning by U.S. journalists, since it would reveal whether Trump held firm to the longstanding U.S position of avoiding commitment on Taiwan’s future. As a result, there was a virtual blackout of news on the summit’s discussions and outcome.

In fact, Trump chose the occurrence of the Xi visit to take the utterly unprecedented action of blocking access to the White House for three major news outlets: CNN. MS Now and Politico. Predictably, in professional solidarity with the Trump-excluded trio, the entire White House press corps, including Trump-friendly outlets, decided en masse to boycott the event .

We may never know whether Trump’s intent here, but Xi could not have been more delighted at the turn of events: He got his status-affirming White House welcome and avoided having to deal with the pesky American media. As the Chinese like to say, it was a win-win — but both wins went to China.

It remains to be seen whether the news blackout hid a more substantive Xi victory on the matter of Taiwan’s independence or a triumph for Trump, Taiwan and international law on the self-determination of states. In either case, violation of the First Amendment was a further stain on the Trump legacy.

Joseph Bosco served as China country director for the secretary of Defense from 2005 to 2006 and as Asia-Pacific director of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief from 2009 to 2010. He is a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Corean-American Studies, a member of the advisory board of the Global Taiwan Institute and member of the advisory board of the Vandenberg Coalition.

articles.summary: The Republican National Committee announced Tuesday that President Trump will headline a rally in Nebraska, marking the latest stop in his upcoming swing of red states over the next week. articles.body:
The Republican National Committee announced Tuesday that President Trump will headline a rally in Nebraska, marking the latest stop in his upcoming swing of red states over the next week.

Trump will make a stop in the city of Grand Island, located in central Nebraska. The state, known as a red stronghold, is home to Senate and gubernatorial races this year.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Senate contest as “likely” Republican and the gubernatorial contest “solid” Republican. However, the state’s Senate race has received more attention as rising energy prices under the Trump administration threaten Republicans in agriculture-centric states.

Decision Desk HQ gives incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts an 81 percent chance of beating independent Dan Osbourne in the Senate race.

The president’s stop in Nebraska is the latest campaign stop in a red state roughly a month out from the midterms. On Thursday, Trump will headline a rally in Durant, Okla. after making a stop at a truck factory in Texas. Trump will then campaign in Mobile, Ala. on Friday before heading to Vandalia, Oh. on Saturday.

Ohio and Texas both have contested Senate and gubernatorial races in November, but Trump’s moves to visit safely red Alabama and Oklahoma so close to an election have raised eyebrows.

A Republican source told The Hill that the decision for Trump to travel to the red states was not indicative that the races are competitive, instead pointing to the Oklahoma and Alabama rallies’ proximity to the Texas and Florida media markets.

Trump announced earlier this month that he would visit 35 competitive races in 30 days ahead of the midterms.

articles.title: Jack Smith spars with GOP senators
articles.summary: Plus: ⚾The road to the World Series begins today {beacon} It’s Tuesday. Are the VMAs old news? Anyone else still seeing Yung Lean and GENER8ION’s performance on stage? Absolutely mesmerizing. In today’s issue: RFK Jr., Vance at MAHA Summit Jack Smith faces questions Protect College Sports Act passes Senate MLB playoffs, NHL season…
articles.body:
It’s Tuesday. Are the VMAs old news? Anyone else still seeing Yung Lean and GENER8ION ’s performance on stage? Absolutely mesmerizing .

Protect College Sports Act passes Senate

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz, filling in for Cate today. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com .

Former special counsel Jack Smith testified in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee Tuesday morning, diving into his past investigations into President Trump.

“I stand by my decisions as Special Counsel, including my decision to bring charges against President Trump,” Smith said in his opening statement.

Smith led a team of Justice Department investigators to determine if Trump would face charges in his actions on Jan. 6, 2021, and the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case. Both cases were wound down when Trump was re-elected.

“I made these decisions without regard to President Trump’s political association, activities, beliefs, or candidacy in the 2024 presidential election,” Smith said.

Republicans made the counter case: Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) bashed Smith over his subpoenas issued as a part of his investigation into the president.

The subpoenas were used to track finances for conservative groups who sponsored and organized events surrounding the Jan. 6 events and election challenges.

“I can tell you why we issued subpoenas, and it was to conduct a criminal investigation of one of the most serious crimes that’s ever happened in our nation’s history.” Smith said to Grassley. In return, Grassley stated that “Donations to Republican groups wasn’t necessary for your investigation, which is proved out by the fact that it was not mentioned in your public report.”

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) ripped into Smith for seeking phone records of some Republican senators as part of his probe, accusing the attorney of not disclosing the requests to the judge overseeing his investigation.

“You make me want to throw up in my mouth,” Kennedy said, after repeatedly cutting off Smith.

Partisan problem: Smith told the Senate Judiciary Committee that he didn’t understand why Republicans thought the investigation into Trump was a partisan effort.

“One of the reasons [Trump] was not able to take power, even though he was seeking to do these things, is because Republicans stood up,” he said.

Smith noted that Former Arizona House speaker Rusty Bowers and former Vice President Mike Pence, “did the right thing and put the interests of the country over the personal interests of Donald Trump” into the investigation.

Smith previously testified before the House Judiciary Committee in January on the matter.

On Monday night, the Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act, which makes various changes, including a cap on how much money in name, image and likeness (NIL) is being dished out to college athletes.

The Senate passed the bill 77-22, with President Trump calling it a “really big deal” on Truth Social .

“It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves,” Trump continued .

Not just an NIL cap: According to The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo , the bill provides the NCAA with federal antitrust protection from lawsuits around the organization’s rule enforcement.

The Protect College Sports Act also emphasizes the recent trends in conference realignment, enforcing a minimum revenue share for big programs where football and basketball rake in a lot more money than smaller programs.

Additionally, the bill guarantees scholarships for 10 years after eligibility and gives athletes the opportunity to transfer once during their college career without having to sit out for a year.

Who wanted this passed? : It was a bipartisan effort led by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.).

Several conferences, including the Southeastern Conference (SEC) and Big Ten, endorsed the bill in July.

Who wants it dead: Democratic Sens. Cory Booker (N.J.) and Chris Murphy (Conn.) were two major critics of the bill, saying that it does not benefit student athletes, but rather the coaches getting paid and universities making money.

“This is a bill not about student athletes, it’s about wealthy coaches and wealthy institutions and an NCAA who has enjoyed unbridled power for decades as we watch discrimination and hardships [for student athletes],” Booker said on Monday.

Organizations such as the NAACP, the AFL-CIO ad the Congressional Black Caucus have raised red flags over the bill’s lack of emphasis on worker protections and who determines the future of Black athletes, coaches and agents and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs).

It now heads to the House, where it won’t be taken up until after the midterms.

Tuesday’s Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Summit touts speakers like Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr ., Vice President Vance and former boxing heavyweight Mike Tyson.

Leaders from the government, healthcare, agriculture and business worlds are gathering to discuss approaches to improving health across the country.

Packed agenda: There are 17 programs scheduled, including “Psychedelic Medicine, the Next Frontier,” “AI and Healthcare,” and “The MAHA Athlete.”

Russell Brand , a comedian expected to go to trial in London next month after pleading not guilty to three counts of rape, is moderating a panel with Mehmet Oz , administrator of Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and Director of Medicaid Dan Brillman .

The day will end with an “exciting announcement” by the health secretary’s wife Cheryl Hines , and then a fireside chat between Vance and RFK Jr.

Here as friends: Health insurers are attending the summit to express that they are partners, not enemies, in making healthcare more accessible affordable.

Axios reports that UnitedHealth, Elevance and AHIP, a health insurance trade association, are set to participate in a panel with a top Medicare official.

Their appearance comes as health insurers have received bipartisan criticism amongst lawmakers and congressional candidates who vow to make healthcare more affordable and blame big companies for the inaccessibility.

Some people aren’t happy: Robert Malone, a former member of RFK Jr.’s vaccine advisory panel, said in a Substack post he was “genuinely taken aback” by the speaker list.

He said that the day is not devoted to the “physicians, scientists, farmers, parents, patients, medical-freedom advocates and independent researchers,” who spent years building the MAHA Movement.

“Instead, the program is heavily populated by executives from some of the largest health-care corporations in America, major hospital systems, health insurers, technology companies, venture-backed medical businesses and companies whose fortunes may depend upon decisions being made by the very federal agencies represented at the conference,” Malone wrote.

Pope Leo XIV said discussions need to be had about how to regulate artificial intelligence, emphasizing that it is one of the biggest challenges we are facing today.

“If someone were to ask me, ‘Am I in panic mode?’ No, I’m not. I sleep at night. I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI should be taken seriously,” the pope told reporters Monday while leaving France for Vatican City.

“I don’t think that, that his is ‘fake news’ as some have said to try and cause whether financial or some other kind of benefit,” Leo continued.

The pope has been in the middle of the AI discussion since the conclave elected him, with him raising concerns on the technology shortly after he was elected.

Latest cause for concern: In recent weeks, rogue AI software has attempted multiple hacks on federal websites including the Department of Education and the Securities and Exchange Commission and Census Bureau, OpenAI revealed over the weekend.

Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon has warned that there is “not enough time” for tech employees to consider the risks of what they are working on.

President Trump launched America.gov on Tuesday, a website that will use AI to help Americans find federal information.

“It’s the ultimate product. It’s called America when you think about it,” Trump said at the launch event . “With America.gov, the federal government no longer stands in your way, and it stands only at your service. And that’s what we’re doing. We’re simplifying it. We’re glamorizing it. We’re making it what it should be.”

Trump has said in recent weeks he is not worried about AI development and will refer to it was “super intelligence” moving forward.

The Trump administration’s ban on $1 billion worth of Canadian goods went into effect on Tuesday. Restrictions were placed on dairy products, alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles.

Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), Tim Kaine (Va.) and Peter Welch (Vt.) are warning the Trump administration against interference ahead of Brazil’s presidential elections, according to a letter obtained exclusively by The Hill.

Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp signed an executive order to suspend the state’s gas tax for 30 days as prices soar due to the Iran war. The order went into effect at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, suspending the 33.3 cents per gallon tax on gasoline and 37.3 cents per gallon tax on diesel.

Two Navy aviators were ejected as they landed their plane on a carrier off the coast of Virginia Monday evening. Two aviators assigned to Carrier Air Wing 3 ejected from their aircraft and four sailors on the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower were injured, the U.S. military said.

articles.title: The ‘swamp’s’ biggest growth industry is lobbying
articles.summary: Lobbying spending reached record levels during President Trump’s second term due to his administration’s expansive tariffs, industrial policies, and regulatory changes.
articles.body:
President Trump’s policies have led to an explosion of spending on lobbying — and, of course, the political donations and potential corruption that come with it. It’s “the swamp” he always talks about, but on steroids.

The bad news for the country, which is good news for lobbyists, is that we will likely see even more lobbying activity as Trump’s tariffs and industrial policies expand in his last two years.

Lobbying is a constitutionally protected activity established in the First Amendment . “Congress shall make no law respecting… the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.” Citizens of a democratic society need the ability to “petition the Government” about matters of concern, especially when government’s actions affect them.

There is a positive side to lobbying. Some lobbyists are experts in their fields and can provide elected officials and bureaucrats with important information and insights that can improve any potential legislation.

But most Americans have a negative view, believing it smacks of favoritism, influence-peddling and even vote-buying. For example, the Pew Research Center wrote in 2023, “Majorities in both parties also say lobbyists, special interests and large employers in lawmakers’ districts have too much influence.”

Yet the sad fact is the more money the government spends and inserts itself into all aspects of our lives — and politicians from both parties are increasingly doing more of both — the more those affected will spend on lobbying to gain their preferred outcome.

According to Open Secrets , a nonprofit organization that tracks lobbying, Trump’s first year back in office saw the most money ever spent on lobbying: $5.13 billion. That was a 15.4 percent increase in spending over President Biden’s last year in office. And 2026 looks like it could surpass 2025, with $2.72 billion spent in the first two quarters.

Spending on lobbying remained relatively flat for a decade, from $3.5 billion in 2010 to $3.53 billion in 2020. Spending increased slightly each of Biden’s four years in the White House, from $3.78 billion to $4.45 billion. But it was bound to explode once Trump got in office because his spending, tariffs and regulatory changes negatively impact almost every industry and consumer — not to mention almost every other country.

Here’s how the system works: Once a president or Congress decides to take steps, either by an executive order or through legislation, that affect industries, companies, organizations or consumers, those affected will reach out to their trade associations and lobbying groups for assistance. The lobbyists begin working the issue, often encouraging their clients to make contributions to the appropriate elected officials. Key people may travel to Washington to meet with elected officials and their staffs, often wining and dining, in order to explain their side of the issue. This activity can go on for months, or years, and cost thousands if not millions of dollars. The money does not necessarily buy a vote, but it often buys access. We’re seeing all of that in the current debate over artificial intelligence and crypto currencies.

Trump’s tariffs affect a large swath of companies and consumers. So, spending on lobbying began increasing early last year. And understandably so. If you run a major company, new tariffs or regulations could force you to lay off hundreds or even thousands of employees. Or you could be forced to raise prices, making it even harder for consumers to buy your product or service. Kelly Blue Book reports Trump’s tariffs imposed on the automotive industry an extra $30 billion in additional costs, leading to an average retail price increase of 10.4 percent.

A CEO has a right, even a duty, to challenge arbitrary and unjust legislation or regulations that could undermine his or her company and the jobs that depend on it.

Which government agencies are receiving most of the lobbyists’ attention? Bloomberg reports for 2025, “The largest increases in filings targeted the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, the Office of the Vice President of the U.S., and the National Economic Council.” No surprises there.

In addition, if the government is handing out lots of taxpayer money — and the Trump administration is — many companies pay lobbyists to reach out to the right people to ensure the companies get a share.

Of course, some companies are bypassing lobbyists because they’ve discovered a shortcut. They’re reportedly making the president’s sons, Eric and Don Jr. , an advisor or board member, paying them very lucrative sums even when they have little expertise. Soon we read some of those companies were awarded a major government contract.

As mentioned previously, this free flow of money doesn’t necessarily lead to corruption, but it can. More importantly, voters increasingly think it does. Gallup recently reported , “Americans’ perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of U.S. adults saying it is widespread.”

Trump’s past pledge to “drain the swamp” now seems so 2016. The swamp — which is often associated with lobbying and influence peddling — has never been bigger, or swampier. Trump likes to mention all the industries he says are doing so well under his administration. Maybe he should include lobbying.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.
